480mkv.py: Write a Python script that takes a text file path as a command-line argument, reads its contents as UTF-8, and filters the lines to keep only those that point to video files in either MKV or MP4 format at the lowest available resolution: it should prefer 480p if any line mentions it, and otherwise fall back to 720p. Ignore blank or whitespace-only lines. Overwrite the original file so it contains only the matching lines, joined by newlines, and print to the console how many matching links were found. The script should handle the case where no lines match by still reporting a count of zero, and it should be robust to typical file paths and encoding of the input file. ---

7ziper.py: Write a Python script that compresses a directory tree or a set of files into 7z archives, with configurable compression levels and automatic handling of already-compressed content. The tool should be a command-line utility that accepts a source path (file or folder), an output archive location, and options that control compression strength, the choice of compression method, and whether to perform a fast or thorough ("full") compression mode. Core behavior to implement: - Accept a file or directory as input and produce a 7z archive at the specified output path. Preserve the relative directory structure inside the archive. - Skip files whose extensions indicate they are already compressed or archival (for example, existing archives, compressed streams, and package wheels), so they are stored rather than recompressed. Support a basic skip list and an extended ("full") skip list that also covers additional formats, selectable via a command-line flag. - Provide a named-method option allowing the user to choose among common 7z compression methods (such as LZMA2, LZMA, or PPMd), with a sensible default. - Offer a "full" high-compression mode that applies strong, solid-archive settings with a large dictionary and block size, intended for maximum compression of large trees. - Use parallel processing to speed up compression of many files where safe, and fall back gracefully to single-process operation when parallelism is not beneficial or not supported. - Use memory-efficient reading for large files where appropriate. - Provide a logging system that reports progress and warnings to the console. Use a richer logging library when available, and fall back to the standard logging facility otherwise. - Handle errors robustly: report missing paths, permission problems, unreadable files, and corrupt or incompatible inputs with clear messages, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up temporary files and partial outputs on failure. - Support temporary working directories for intermediate staging, removed automatically at the end. - Optionally support tar-based intermediate packaging when it helps preserve metadata such as permissions and timestamps. - Print a concise summary at the end: number of files processed, number skipped, original versus compressed size, compression ratio, and elapsed time. - Validate arguments before doing any work (for example, refusing to overwrite an existing output without an explicit flag, and checking that the chosen method and level are valid). - Keep the command-line interface self-documenting with help text, and make the script runnable directly as a standalone program. ---

a-b.py: Write a Python script that takes two text file paths from the command line: a target file and a reference file. The script should remove from the target file every line that also appears (exactly, ignoring trailing newline characters) anywhere in the reference file, leaving all other lines untouched and in their original order. The target file must be updated in place, and the rewrite should be safe: write the filtered result to a temporary location first and then replace the original so a failure mid-write does not corrupt the target. Read and write all text as UTF-8. Preserve the original line endings of the kept lines. The script should run as a standalone command-line tool, exit cleanly on success, and handle the case where the reference file has no lines or where no lines match by simply leaving the target content intact (or unchanged). Keep the implementation simple and idiomatic, and do not print anything other than what is necessary for errors. ---

abline.py: Write a Python script that runs from the command line and processes a text file line by line, based on a chosen mode and a user-supplied delimiter character. The script should accept three arguments: a mode flag, the path to an input text file, and a single target character or delimiter. The mode flag selects one of two behaviors: in the first mode, each non-empty line is trimmed of surrounding whitespace and, if it contains the delimiter, only the portion before the first occurrence of the delimiter is kept; in the second mode, each non-empty line is trimmed and, if it contains the delimiter, only the portion after the first occurrence of the delimiter is kept. Lines that do not contain the delimiter should be kept in full after trimming. Lines that become empty as a result of processing should be discarded. The script should read the file using UTF-8 encoding, handle the file's lines robustly, and collect all non-empty results. The final output should be the collected results printed to standard output, one result per line, preserving their original order. The script should be a simple, self-contained tool with a clear invocation pattern and should handle missing or malformed arguments gracefully by showing a brief usage message rather than crashing. ---

add2lines.py: Write a Python script that takes two command-line arguments: the path to a text file and a prefix string. The script should validate that exactly two arguments are supplied, printing a brief usage message to standard error and exiting with a non-zero status if not. It should confirm the given path refers to an existing regular file, reporting an error to standard error and exiting with a non-zero status otherwise. When the input is valid, the script should prepend the prefix string, followed by a single space, to every non-blank line in the file, leaving blank or whitespace-only lines unchanged. The original line endings and overall file structure must be preserved. The modified content should be saved back to the same file, replacing the original contents. On success, the script should print a short confirmation message that includes the file path, indicating the file was updated. ---

add_hints.py: Write a Python script that acts as an automated type-annotation assistant for existing Python source files. The tool should take a path to a Python file (or a directory of Python files) as input and produce type-annotated versions of the code without changing its runtime behavior. It should work by analyzing the source's syntax tree to find function parameters, return positions, and variables that lack type hints, then infer likely types from several signals: literal values assigned or passed as defaults, common naming conventions (for example, names like "count", "index", or "verbose" suggesting integers or booleans), and simple usage patterns within the code. Where a type can be confidently inferred, the tool should add the annotation; where it cannot, it should leave the code alone rather than guess wildly. The script should preserve the original formatting, comments, and layout as much as possible so that the diff between the original and the annotated output is minimal and easy to review. It should ensure any needed type imports (such as those from the typing module) are added to the file automatically and only when required. Provide a command-line interface that accepts the target path and options such as a dry-run mode that prints a unified diff of proposed changes without writing files, a verbose mode that explains each inferred annotation, a flag to write changes in place, and an option to write results to a separate output location. When writing in place, the tool should keep a backup of the original file. It should handle errors gracefully, skipping files that fail to parse and reporting a summary at the end listing how many files were processed, modified, and skipped, along with any problems encountered. The script should be robust to common Python constructs including nested functions, class methods, decorators, and async functions, and it should never introduce syntax errors into the output. Include a clear help message describing usage and options. ---

addmainguard.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree for Python source files and ensures each one has a standard `__main__` entry point guard, adding the missing scaffolding where needed. The tool should accept a target directory (or individual files) from the command line, along with options to control the number of parallel workers, the indentation style used for generated code, a list of directory names to skip during traversal (with sensible defaults such as version control folders, virtual environments, caches, and build output), and a dry-run mode that reports what would change without modifying any files. For each Python file it examines, the script should parse the source structurally rather than relying solely on text matching, so it can reliably detect whether a proper main guard already exists (recognizing the common comparison form against the module name and the main string, regardless of quote style). If no guard is present, it should append a template consisting of a `main()` function stub with a docstring and placeholder body, followed by a guard block that invokes `main()` and exits with its return value. If a file already contains a main function, the script should avoid creating a duplicate definition and should only add the guard if it is missing. Files that cannot be parsed due to syntax errors should be skipped with a clear warning rather than crashing the run. Processing should be distributed across multiple worker processes for speed, with results collected and summarized at the end: the number of files scanned, files modified, files skipped, and errors encountered. The script should use structured logging with adjustable verbosity, return a meaningful exit code (zero on success, non-zero when errors occur), and print a concise, human-readable report. Preserve the original file encoding and line endings wherever possible, and never leave a file partially written if an error occurs mid-operation. ---

afk.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line code analysis and cleanup tool for Python source files. It should accept one or more file or directory paths (recursively discovering `.py` files while skipping common virtual environment, cache, and version-control folders), along with options that control whether it reports issues only or applies fixes in place, and an option to restrict analysis to certain file patterns or exclusions. The tool should parse each Python file and detect a set of code quality problems, including overly long lines beyond a configurable limit, unused or duplicate imports, unnecessary or sloppy exception handling (such as bare or overly broad excepts and empty handlers), and other common style or correctness smells that can be determined statically. For each issue it finds, it should record the file, line number, a short rule identifier, and a human-readable message. Where a safe automatic fix is possible, the tool should be able to apply it, and it should always preserve the original meaning and syntax of the code. It should also offer a dry-run or diff mode that shows proposed changes in unified diff form without modifying files. Files that cannot be parsed, are binary, or exceed a reasonable size limit should be skipped gracefully with a warning rather than crashing the run. The script should support processing many files efficiently, optionally in parallel across CPU cores, and should be able to read input from standard input for stdin-based workflows. It should also be able to inspect the contents of compressed or archived sources (such as gzip, bz2, lzma, zip, or tar archives) and report on the Python files within them without extracting them to disk permanently. Output should be available in a human-readable text format by default, with an option for machine-readable JSON output. The tool should set a meaningful exit status: zero when no issues are found, and a non-zero code when issues remain or when errors occurred. It should include clear `--help` documentation with usage examples, validate its arguments, and handle keyboard interrupts and I/O errors cleanly. ---

afkx.py: Write a Python script that scans a Python project (or a single Python file, or an archive containing Python files) and detects unused imports, reporting them and optionally removing them automatically. The tool should accept a file or directory path as input and recursively discover Python source files, skipping common non-source directories such as virtual environments, caches, and version-control folders. It should analyze each file to identify imported names that are never referenced in the code, taking into account aliased imports, `from` imports, wildcard-style cases, and names used only in type annotations or `__all__` exports, which should not be flagged as unused. For each file, the tool should produce a per-file result that includes the list of unused imports, a unified diff showing what a fix would change, and any error encountered while parsing or processing that file. Files that cannot be parsed should be reported gracefully without stopping the whole run. Provide a command-line interface that supports a dry-run mode (report only, no changes), an apply mode that rewrites files in place with the unused imports removed while preserving the rest of the code's formatting and comments as much as possible, and an option to create backups before modifying files. Allow users to control output verbosity, disable colored output (automatically detect when the terminal does not support it), and choose between human-readable text and machine-readable JSON output. Processing of multiple files should be able to run concurrently to improve speed on large projects, with a configurable number of workers. The tool should also be able to read archived inputs such as zip and tar files, analyzing the Python files inside them without extracting them to disk permanently, and should handle optional compression formats gracefully when their supporting libraries are not installed. The script should exit with a meaningful status code: zero when no unused imports are found, a non-zero code when unused imports are reported in dry-run mode, and a distinct code when errors occurred. It should print a concise summary at the end including counts of files scanned, files with issues, total unused imports found, and files modified. ---

aitrans.py: Write a Python script that acts as a universal, command-line text translation tool supporting multiple AI translation backends. The script should load configuration such a user-levelment file in the home directory (ignoring blank lines and comments, and stripping surrounding quotes from values), and fall back to real environment variables when needed. It should support at least two AI providers (an OpenAI-compatible service and Google's Gemini service), initialize only the clients whose SDKs and credentials are available, and degrade gracefully with clear messages when a provider or dependency is missing. The tool should accept input from the command line, including a source file path, a glob pattern to process multiple files, or direct text, along with target language, optional source language (auto-detect by default), and a choice of provider and model. It should translate the content while preserving its original structure, formatting, line breaks, code blocks, markup, and placeholders, and write results to an output file or directory, or print them to standard output. Batch processing of many files should be supported, with per-file error handling so one failure does not stop the rest, and a concise summary of successes and failures at the end. Behavior requirements: validate all arguments and file paths before making API calls, provide helpful error messages and non-zero exit codes on failure, avoid overwriting existing files unless explicitly allowed, handle large inputs by chunking when necessary while keeping translations coherent, and never print secrets such as API keys. The script should be runnable as a standalone program with a `--help` description of its usage. ---

alu.py: Write a Python script that checks the system's package manager for software packages that have available updates, extracts just the package names from the results, saves that list to a text file at a fixed location on an Android-style storage path, and prints each package name to the console as a bullet-pointed list. Requirements: - Run the system's package listing command for upgradable packages, suppressing its raw output, and capture the text result. - Process the output line by line: for lines that contain a package identifier with a source suffix (separated by a slash), keep only the portion before that separator; for other non-empty lines that are not header or status messages (such as lines mentioning "Listing"), keep the whole trimmed line. - Ignore blank lines and skip informational header text. - If at least one package name was collected, write all names to the target file as UTF-8 text, one name per line, overwriting any previous content. - Display each collected name on the console, prefixed by an indented dash, so the user sees the same list that was saved. - If no packages are found, do not create or modify the output file and print nothing extra. - The script should run as a standalone program using a conventional main entry point. ---

annotate.py: Write a Python script that acts as a type-annotation assistant for existing Python source files. The tool should take one or more Python files or directories as input, analyze their function and method signatures, and automatically add or refine type annotations so the code is more explicit about the types it accepts and returns. Key requirements: - **Purpose:** Infer missing parameter and return type annotations for functions in the target code, using a stub or type-inference source where available, and write the improved code back without changing its runtime behavior. - **Inputs:** A path (file or directory) containing Python source, plus command-line options such as whether to modify files in place, whether to preview changes, and which stub or type-information sources to use. - **Outputs:** Updated Python files with annotations inserted, or a unified diff preview showing exactly what would change. The tool should report a summary of how many annotations were added and which files were skipped or failed. - **Safety behaviors:** Preserve original formatting and comments as much as possible. Never alter function bodies or logic. Validate that each modified file still parses correctly before saving, and leave the original file untouched if the transformation fails. - **Stub cleanup:** When type information comes from typeshed-style stub files, sanitize references to private or stub-only modules (such as the `_typeshed` module) so the output imports only standard, runnable names from `typing` or the standard library. - **Robustness:** Handle large codebases by processing files independently, so that one failing file does not stop the whole run. Allow a configurable degree of parallelism and a timeout per file. - **Command-line interface:** Provide clear help text, sensible defaults, and meaningful exit codes that indicate success, partial failure, or a usage error. - **Logging:** Give concise progress output, with a verbose mode for detailed diagnostics about which functions were annotated and why any were skipped. ---

annotate_types.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for automatically adding type annotations to an existing Python source file. The tool should take a target Python file path as input, along with options that control whether changes are applied directly to the file or only previewed. It should use a type-inference step based on available type stub information to determine annotations for function parameters and return values, then rewrite the source so the annotations are inserted while preserving the original formatting, comments, and structure as much as possible. Key behaviors to include: - Accept a file path (and optionally a directory or multiple files) as input via command-line arguments, with a flag to write changes in place versus printing a unified diff of the proposed modifications. - Run a type-inference pass that produces candidate annotations, then apply them to the source code without changing program behavior. - Sanitize any inferred annotations that reference private or stub-only modules (such as typeshed-internal names) by replacing them with valid runtime-importable equivalents, such as the standard typing module, so the resulting file remains importable. - Ensure any needed imports (e.g., for type names used in the new annotations) are added to the file and that existing imports are preserved. - Skip or safely handle files that fail to parse, reporting clear error messages without crashing the entire run when processing multiple files. - Report a summary at the end, such as the number of files processed, files changed, and annotations added. - Use a temporary working area for intermediate processing so the original file is never left in a corrupted state if an error occurs mid-run. - Exit with a non-zero status code if errors occurred, and zero otherwise. The tool should be robust, well-structured, and suitable for use in a developer workflow or as a step in a CI pipeline, with clear help text describing all options. ---

ans2proj.py: Write a Python script that reads a Markdown document and extracts embedded file contents from it, then recreates those files on disk as a project tree. The script should accept a path to a Markdown file as input and an output directory where the extracted files will be written. Each file in the Markdown is marked by a level-two heading that contains a relative file path wrapped in backticks, followed by a fenced code block holding that file's contents. The script should locate every such heading, pair it with the first code fence beneath it, and capture the enclosed text as the file body, correctly handling fences with or without language tags, trailing whitespace, and both Unix and Windows line endings. If a heading has no code block beneath it, the script should log a warning and skip that entry without stopping. The script should create any necessary parent directories, write each extracted file using UTF-8 encoding, and preserve the content exactly as it appears inside the fence, without adding or stripping meaningful whitespace beyond the trailing newline that precedes the closing fence. It should guard against path traversal by refusing to write any file whose resolved location falls outside the chosen output directory, logging an error for such entries instead. Use a structured logging approach to report progress, including the number of files successfully written, warnings for malformed or skipped sections, and errors for failed writes. The script should run from the command line, print a clear summary at the end, and exit with a nonzero status code if the input file is missing, unreadable, or if no valid file sections are found. Handle encoding and I/O errors gracefully with informative messages rather than unhandled tracebacks. ---

appender.py: Write a Python script that reads the full contents of a text file named "prompt.txt" located in the user's home directory, then appends that content to the end of every existing .txt file in the current working directory. The script should process each matching file independently, preserving each file's original content and adding the prompt text after it, with all reading and writing done using UTF-8 encoding. For each file, it should report success with a clear status message showing the file name, or report a failure message including the file name and the reason, so that an error in one file does not stop processing of the remaining files. The script should only run its main behavior when executed directly rather than when imported as a module. ---

archive_convert.py: Write a Python script that acts as a batch archive compression tool for a directory tree. The script should accept a root directory (or a set of paths) and recursively find files that are candidates for compression, then compress each one into several archive formats in parallel, reporting the size savings for each output. Core behavior: - Walk a given directory tree, skipping version-control metadata directories (such as `.git`), and process every regular file found. Files that are already archives or compressed outputs produced by the tool should be ignored to avoid re-processing. - For each input file, produce compressed variants using multiple codecs and container formats, including common ones such as gzip, bzip2, xz/LZMA, zip, and Brotli, with tar-based wrappers where appropriate (for example tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.bz2, tgz, tbz2, txz, zip). Some formats may depend on optional external tools or libraries; the script should detect availability and gracefully skip unavailable formats with a clear log message. - Choose compression levels sensibly: use maximum-effort settings for small files and faster, lower-effort settings for large files (for example above roughly 10 MB) so that processing remains practical. Use a configurable chunk size for streaming large files rather than loading them fully into memory. - Run compression jobs concurrently across multiple worker processes, with a configurable number of workers (default around 8). Each job should write to a temporary location and atomically move the result into place only on success, so partial outputs never remain behind on failure. - Skip outputs that already exist and are up to date, and allow the user to force regeneration via a flag. - Support a dry-run mode that reports what would be done without writing any files. - Provide a command-line interface with options for the target path, number of jobs, format selection or exclusion, force overwrite, dry-run, and verbosity level. - Log progress and results using a structured logging approach. For each produced archive, report the original size, the compressed size, and the percentage saved in human-readable units (B, KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB). At the end, print a summary with totals, number of files processed, number of failures, and total space saved. - Handle errors robustly: a failure in one file or one format must not abort the whole run; collect failures, report them at the end, and returnonzero exit status if any job failed. - Respect Ctrl+C by cleanly terminating worker processes and removing any temporary files. The script should be a self-contained, production-quality command-line utility with clear help text, sensible defaults, and well-structured code that is easy to extend with additional compression formats. ---

archive_dir.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line utility for archiving a directory into a tar or compressed tar.gz file. The user supplies the path to an existing folder as the main input, and optionally an output file path; if no output path is given, the archive is placed beside the source folder and named after it, with a .tar extension for uncompressed archives or .tar.gz for compressed ones. The tool should let the user choose the compression mode and should validate the input carefully: expand user home shortcuts, resolve the path to an absolute location, and produce clear, human-readable error messages when the folder does not exist or the path is not a directory. The script should also support an optional cleanup step that removes the original source folder after a successful archive is created. This deletion must be cautious: it should refuse to delete symbolic links that point to directories, avoid removing the output archive itself, and only proceed once the archive has been written completely and verified as readable. Provide a safety confirmation mechanism (for example, an interactive prompt with a bypass flag for automation) before any destructive action. Where it is useful for large folders, the script may parallelize work using multiple processes, with a user-configurable worker count that must be a positive integer; the argument parser should reject values below one. Errors during archiving should be reported without leaving a corrupt or partial output file behind, and the script should exit with a non-zero status code on failure and zero on success. Keep the interface clean and self-documenting with a help message, and print concise progress or result information to the console. ---

archive_merger.py: Write a Python script that compresses a given folder into a tar-based archive, supporting both plain tar and gzip-compressed tar output, with an optional step that removes the original folder after successful archiving. The tool should be runnable from the command line and accept the target folder path as its primary input, along with optional arguments for specifying a custom output archive location, choosing the compression mode, and enabling cleanup of the source directory. Where practical, it should take advantage of multiple workers to speed up compression of large folder trees, while still producing a single valid archive file. The script should resolve paths to absolute form, create parent output locations as needed, and report progress and the final archive path to the user via console messages. It must handle errors gracefully, such as missing folders, permission problems, or failed writes, by printing a clear message and returning a non-zero exit status, and it should only delete the original folder if the archive was created successfully. The overall behavior should be robust, readable, and suitable for use in backup or archival workflows. ---

ccss.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line CSS minifier batch tool. It should accept one or more CSS file paths as command-line arguments; if no arguments are given, it should automatically discover all CSS files (including minified CSS files) in the current working directory. For each file, the script should skip files that don't exist or that consist of only a single line, and otherwise run an external CSS optimization utility at a high optimization level with options that remove unused or duplicate rules, overwriting the file in place. Report progress to the console as it works: print each file name, then a status indicator showing whether the file was optimized (with the amount of bytes saved and the percentage of size reduction, shown in a distinct color), whether no change occurred, or whether an error happened (shown in red). Before processing begins, record the total size of the working directory, and after all files are processed, report the overall size savings in a clear summary. Handle failures gracefully so that an error on one file does not stop processing of the remaining files, and ensure the script reports human-readable file sizes throughout. ---

chafaer.py: Write a Python script that displays an image directly in a terminal using colored text blocks. The script should take an image file path as its command-line input, open the image, and render it so that it fits the current terminal window while preserving the original aspect ratio. Each character cell should represent two vertically stacked pixels, using a half-block character whose foreground and background colors carry the top and bottom pixel colors, with full 24-bit true-color output. The rendered result should be printed to standard output as a series of text lines, with proper color resets at the end of each line so the terminal display stays clean. The script should automatically detect the terminal's dimensions, leave a small margin at the bottom so output does not scroll awkwardly, and scale the image down with high-quality resampling when it is larger than the available space. Handle the case where the image is not in RGB mode by converting it first, and ensure the output works for both wide and tall images. The script should run only when executed directly as a main program and should be designed as a simple, self-contained command-line utility for previewing images in a terminal. ---

change_project_name.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line bulk find-and-replace refactoring tool for a project directory. It takes two arguments from the command line: the text to search for and the replacement text. If the wrong number of arguments is supplied, it should print a brief usage message showing the expected format and exit with a non-zero status. Starting from the current working directory, the script should recursively walk through all files and folders in the project tree. For every readable text file, it should replace every occurrence of the search text with the replacement text, saving the file in UTF-8 encoding. Files that cannot be decoded as text, or that the script lacks permission to read or write, should be skipped silently without stopping the overall process. In addition to updating file contents, the script should rename files and directories whose names contain the search text, substituting the replacement text in the name. Renaming should be performed carefully: if a target name already exists, the script must not overwrite it, and should instead print a clear message telling the user to resolve the conflict manually and leave that item unchanged. Any unexpected error during a rename should be handled gracefully so the script continues processing the remaining items. Processing order should be safe for a tree being modified while it is traversed, so that renaming a directory does not break the processing of its children. The script should produce no output for successful routine replacements beyond what is needed for conflict warnings and errors, and should be designed to run cleanly on Windows, macOS, and Linux. ---

check_conflicts.py: Write a Python script that audits the packages installed in the current Python environment for naming conflicts with the standard library and with a known list of PyPI package names, then produces a machine-readable conflict report. The script should: Read a JSON file containing a list of known PyPI package names (entries may be plain strings or lists/tuples whose first element is the name). If this file is missing, it should print a warning to stderr and continue with the PyPI check skipped rather than failing. - Gather the names of all currently installed distributions, normalizing them so that differences in case and in separators (hyphens, underscores, dots) are treated as equivalent. - Compare the installed package names against the Python standard library module names and against the PyPI name list, flagging any installed package whose name shadows or collides with one of them. - Accept command-line options that let the user specify the PyPI names file location and the output report path, with sensible defaults for both. - Write the results to a JSON report file summarizing each detected conflict, including the offending package name, the kind of conflict (standard library shadowing or PyPI name collision), and enough detail for a user to act on it. - Print a concise human-readable summary to the console indicating how many conflicts were found and where the report was saved. - Handle errors gracefully: malformed or unreadable input files should produce clear error messages, and the script should exit with a non-zero status when a fatal problem occurs and zero when the audit completes. - Be runnable directly from the command line as a standalone tool, with a clear help message describing its options. ---

check_exports.py: Scan Python files for top-level public definitions. Accepts one or more files or directories. With no arguments, processes '.' recursively. Skips symlinks and common non-source directories (.git, __pycache__, .venv, node_modules, build, dist, ...). For each file, lists public functions (including async), classes, and module-level constants. When a file lives in a package (i.e. a sibling __init__.py exists), also flags definitions that are not exported from __init__.py, and can autofix them with -a.

check_fname_conflict.py: Write a Python script that scans the current working directory and reports which Python files depend on third-party packages that are not listed in a known requirements file. The script should read a pip-style list of installed or required package names from a fixed location on the device, normalize the package names (ignoring version specifiers, comments, and blank lines, treating hyphens and underscores as equivalent and comparing case-insensitively), and build a set of known third-party packages. If that file is missing, the script should warn the user on the error stream and continue, skipping the third-party comparison. The script should also determine which modules are part of the standard library so they can be excluded from the dependency check, and it should warn if the running Python version does not provide the standard library module list. Its main job is to recursively examine the Python source files in the target directory, identify the top-level modules each file imports, and classify each import as standard library, locally defined, or third-party. It should then report the imports that are neither standard library nor covered by the known package list, giving the user a clear summary of potentially missing dependencies, along with the file names where they occur. The output should be human-readable, using short status messages with emoji-style prefixes to show progress (for example, announcing the directory being scanned and the number of entries loaded), and it should end with a concise summary of findings. The script should handle unreadable or non-UTF-8 files gracefully without crashing, skip hidden and virtual-environment directories where appropriate, and exit with a clear, meaningful status code indicating whether any unlisted third-party dependencies were found. ---

check_funcs.py: Write a Python script that scans a given Python source file and produces a structured summary of its public top-level definitions. The tool should accept a file path as input, safely read and parse the file's source without executing it, and identify all publicly exposed top-level functions (including asynchronous ones), classes, and constant-style module-level assignments, ignoring any names that are private (prefixed with an underscore). The output should be a categorized listing of these names, grouped into functions, classes, and constants, so that a developer can quickly understand the public API surface of the module. The script must handle failure gracefully: if the file cannot be decoded, contains syntax errors, or cannot be read for any other reason, it should log a clear error message describing the problem and return an empty but well-formed result rather than crashing. check_main_guard.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree and reports which Python source files are missing a standard entry-point guard (the `if __name__ == "__main__":` idiom). clean-bash.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for automatically reformatting and tidying Bash shell scripts across a directory tree. The tool should accept one or more file or directory paths as input, recursively discover Bash scripts within them, and identify them by either a `.sh` extension or, for extensionless files, a shebang line referencing bash or sh. clean-cpp.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree of C and C++ source files and identifies all comments in each file, using a syntax-aware parser so that comment detection is accurate (ignoring comment-like text inside string literals). The tool should accept a root path (file or directory) as a command-line argument, recursively discover source and header files by their common C/C++ extensions (such as .c, .h, .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .hpp, .hh, .hxx, .inl), and process them in parallel using a configurable number of worker processes to keep throughput high on large codebases. clean-css.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line CSS minifier and comment-stripper for entire project directories. Key behaviors: - Walk a directory tree recursively to find CSS files, skipping common non-source folders such as version control metadata, virtual environments, dependency folders, IDE settings, caches, and build output directories. - Process files in parallel across available CPU cores to handle large projects efficiently. - Parse each stylesheet with a robust syntax-aware approach so that comments are identified accurately, including ones inside strings or unusual constructs. Files that fail to parse cleanly should be left untouched or reported rather than corrupted. - Remove all comments and collapse redundant whitespace, while keeping strings, URLs, and selectors valid. Optionally apply a more aggressive compression pass when an optional third-party minifier is available, and fall back gracefully to a built-in approach when it is not installed. - Skip empty files without error. - Support a dry-run mode that reports which files would change and shows a unified diff of the proposed edits, without writing anything. - Support an in-place mode that overwrites the original files, and an output mode that writes minified copies to a separate destination directory while preserving the relative folder structure. - Optionally create a backup of each original file before overwriting it. - Report a clear summary at the end: number of files scanned, processed, skipped, and failed, plus total bytes saved and percentage reduction. - Handle errors per file so that one bad stylesheet never stops the whole run, and exit with a non-zero status code if any failures occurred. - Provide a clear command-line interface with help text, validation of paths, and sensible defaults; the user should be able to choose the target path, mode, output location, and whether to back up files. ---

clean-html.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line minifier for web source files within a project directory. It should recursively scan a given directory (and accept a target path as input), loc JavaScript files, and produce minified versions of them while preserving their functional behavior. clean-js.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for minifying JavaScript source files in a project directory tree. Core behavior: - Walk a directory recursively, locating JavaScript files, and skip common non-source or build/dependency folders (such as version control, virtual environment, package cache, IDE configuration, and build output directories). - Process files in parallel across available CPU cores to keep large projects fast. - For each file, parse the JavaScript syntax first. clean-lua.py: Write a Python script that removes comments from Lua source files in a directory tree, safely and in parallel, while preserving the code itself. clean_version.py: Write a Python script that takes the path to a text file containing pip freeze output, reads its contents, and rewrites that same file so that it contains only the package names, one per line, with all version pins, direct URL references, VCS links, environment markers, comments, blank lines, and editable-install prefixes removed. cleanbash.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree for Bash shell scripts and strips out their comments while preserving the scripts' executable behavior, writing the cleaned results back to disk. cleaner.py: Write a Python script that cleans up raw terminal or text output captured from a command-line session, removing terminal control noise so the result is readable plain text. cleanhistory.py: Write a Python script that cleans up the user's bash command history file located in their home directory. cleanjsts.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree for JavaScript and TypeScript source files (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx) and removes all comments from them while preserving the code's exact behavior and syntax. cleanlog.py: Write a Python script that cleans up raw terminal output text so it is readable as plain text. cleanlua.py: Write a Python script that process files to remove ordinary comments while preserving documentation comments. cleanpy.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for cleaning up Python source files by stripping comments and docstrings, with the option to preserve certain special comment markers. cleanrs.py: Write a Python script that removes comments from Rust source files in bulk, using a syntax-aware parser so that comment-like text inside string literals, raw strings, and character literals is preserved. cleants.py: Write a Python script that acts as a multi-language comment remover for source code files. Include meaningful error messages for missing paths, unreadable files, and unsupported input, and exit with a non-zero status code if any file failed. ---

cliner.py: Write a Python script that cleans up terminal-captured log files in place by stripping ANSI escape sequences, control characters, and other terminal formatting artifacts, while normalizing excess whitespace. The tool should accept a directory (or a set of paths) as input, locate all log files within it, and process them so that the resulting text is readable plain text with the original line content preserved. Key requirements: - **Scope**: Only target log files with a specific extension. Recurse through subdirectories when given a directory. - **Cleaning rules**: Remove color codes, cursor movement sequences, character set switching codes, carriage returns, shift-in/shift-out control characters, and similar terminal escape artifacts. After removing these, collapse runs of two or more spaces into a single space. Line endings should remain meaningful and the content otherwise untouched. - **Size-aware processing**: Small files should be read and rewritten in a straightforward way. Large files (above roughly 1 MB) should be handled efficiently, using memory-mapped or streaming access so that memory usage stays bounded, and the cleaned output should be written safely (for example, to a temporary file that replaces the original only upon success). - **Parallelism**: Process multiple files concurrently using a small fixed pool of workers (around four) to speed up batch runs. - **Robustness**: Tolerate undecodable bytes by ignoring or replacing them rather than crashing. Any per-file failure should be captured and reported without stopping the rest of the batch. - **Reporting**: After processing, print or return a summary that lists each file processed, whether it succeeded, which processing mode was used, and any error messages, followed by totals for successes and failures. - **Command-line usage**: Provide a simple command-line interface taking the target path(s), with clear help text and a non-zero exit status if any file failed. - **Safety**: Never leave a partially written file in place of an original if processing fails mid-way. ---

cliner2.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans the current working directory and all of its subdirectories for log files (files ending in the ".log" extension), then cleans each one in place by stripping terminal control and escape-sequence artifacts from its contents. The script should: - Search the current directory tree for every file with a ".log" extension and report how many were found. If none are found, print a clear message stating that no log files exist and exit gracefully. - For each discovered log file, read its contents using UTF-8 encoding while silently ignoring any undecodable bytes, so that malformed files do not stop processing. - Remove a predefined set of noise patterns commonly left behind by terminal output and ANSI escape codes. These include ANSI color and cursor control sequences (such as color codes, cursor movement, and character-set selection sequences), carriage return characters, shift-in and shift-out control characters, and stray caret or bracket fragments that result from captured escape sequences. Design the pattern list so it is easy to extend. - After removing those artifacts, collapse runs of two or more consecutive spaces within each line into a single space, while preserving line breaks and the overall line structure. - Overwrite each cleaned file with its sanitized content, writing back using UTF-8 encoding. - Print a concise status message for each file as it is processed: a success indicator with the file path when cleaning succeeds, and an error indicator with the file path and the error description when it fails. A failure on one file must not prevent the remaining files from being processed. - Handle errors robustly so that permission problems, missing files, or encoding issues are reported without crashing the entire run. - Use clear, user-friendly console output so a user can see at a glance how many files were found and what happened to each one. The tool is intended as a simple command-line utility that a user runs from within a project folder to batch-clean terminal-captured log files, making them readable for review or further analysis. ---

codepener.py: Write a Python script that takes a raw HTML body fragment saved in a file and wraps it into a complete, standalone HTML5 document ready for use as a CodePen-style project. The script should read the input file (UTF-8), handling missing-file and read errors gracefully with clear console messages and a failure indication. It should derive a readable page title from the input file's name by default (replacing hyphens with spaces and capitalizing words), while allowing the user to supply a custom title. The generated document must include the proper document declaration, language and character encoding metadata, a responsive viewport setting, and links to external stylesheet and script files named style.css and script.js, with the original fragment placed inside the body. The script should accept the input path, an optional output path, and an optional title from the command line, and by default write the result to a new file alongside the input (or to the specified output path). On success it should report where the output was saved; on failure it should exit with a non-zero status. Keep the tool dependency-free, well-structured, and usable both as a command-line utility and as an importable module with a reusable conversion function. ---

colab1.py: Write a Python script that backs up the installed third-party packages from the current Python environment's site-packages directory into a persistent cloud storage location, designed to run in a Google Colab notebook environment. The script should: - Mount the user's Google Drive so that the output location persists beyond the session. - Create a destination folder in the mounted Drive (creating any missing parent folders) to hold the exported packages. - Scan the top level of the site-packages directory and skip packages that manage the environment itself, specifically anything whose name begins with "setuptools" or "pip". - For individual files found at the top level (such as standalone modules or metadata files), copy them as-is into the destination folder while preserving their timestamps. - For each package directory found, compress its entire contents into a single ZIP archive named after the directory, using deflate compression. Include all files recursively, but exclude compiled Python bytecode files (.pyc). Store paths inside each archive relative to the site-packages root so the archive can be restored correctly. - Track and report how many files were copied and how many directories were archived. - Print a clear success message when the export completes, followed by a summary line showing the site-packages location that was exported and the counts of copied files and archived directories. Keep the script simple, robust, and self-contained, with clear console output and sensible handling of the case where the destination already contains earlier exports (overwriting matching names is acceptable). ---

collect_env_vars.py: Write a Python script that scans every file within the current directory tree (including all nested subdirectories) and collects the names of environment variables defined in those files. An environment variable definition is recognized when a line begins with an uppercase name made of letters, digits, and underscores, immediately followed by an equals sign (for example, a line in a configuration or .env-style file). Read each file as UTF-8 text; if a file cannot be read or decoded, report a brief warning that includes the file path and the reason, then continue processing the remaining files without stopping. Once scanning is complete, gather all unique variable names, sort them alphabetically, and write them to a plain text file named env_vars.txt in the current directory, with one variable name per line. Ensure the output file is written using UTF-8 encoding. When finished, print a single summary message to the console stating how many unique variable names were found and where the results were saved. The script should be self-contained, run from the command line with no required arguments, handle empty directories and files with no matches gracefully (producing an empty output file and a zero count), and avoid crashing on unexpected file system or encoding errors. ---

collect_files.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans the current working directory for files with a user-specified extension (for example, "txt", "pdf", or "jpg") and collects copies of all matching files into a single folder named after that extension, created inside the current directory if it does not already exist. The script should accept the target extension as a command-line argument, tolerate a leading dot in the argument, and exit with a clear usage message when the argument is missing. Key behaviors: - Search all subdirectories of the current working directory, including nested ones, for matching files. - Skip any files that already reside inside the destination folder, so previously collected files are not copied again. - Preserve each file's original metadata such as timestamps and permissions when copying. - Never overwrite existing files in the destination. If a filename collision occurs, append an incrementing numeric suffix before the extension (for example, "report_1.txt", "report_2.txt") until a free name is found. - Print a line for each successful copy showing the original source path and the new destination path. - Handle errors on individual files gracefully: report the failing file and continue processing the rest instead of aborting the whole run. - At the end, print a summary stating how many files were successfully copied. The output is a self-contained, runnable script that performs this collection reliably and safely, with clear console feedback for the user. ---

collectlic.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans a given root directory and gathers the contents of every file whose name contains the word "license" (case-insensitive), then consolidates those contents into a single UTF-8 text file at a fixed output location. The script should skip version-control metadata directories (such as `.git`) entirely, tolerate permission errors and unreadable files without crashing, and never include its own output file in the results. Before writing, it should report how many matching files were found. For each matched file, the consolidated output should clearly separate entries by showing the file's path relative to the scanned root, followed by that file's full text content, so the result reads as a single navigable document. Content that cannot be decoded should be handled gracefully, for example by ignoring problematic characters rather than failing. The script should create any missing parent directories for the output location, overwrite any previous output on each run, and finish without requiring user interaction. Keep the design simple, robust, and self-contained, and ensure it runs as a standalone command-line tool that accepts the target root directory as its input. ---

colortools.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree for color values in text-based source and style files, then either reports them or rewrites them with randomly generated replacement colors. The tool should accept a root path (file or directory) and an option to restrict which file types are processed. It should skip binary files, ignore files or directories that a shared utility marks as excluded when that utility is available, and fall back to simple built-in equivalents when it is not. Recognize color literals in several common notations: short and long hexadecimal codes with a leading hash, bare hex strings that appear in the text, and CSS-style functional color expressions in rgb or rgba form, including those with fractional alpha values. Each match should be handled in a way that preserves the surrounding text and the original notation style as much as practical. Provide a dry-run or report mode that prints each file path, the line numbers, and the colors found, with a summary count at the end. Provide a mode that actually modifies files, generating replacement colors using a hue, saturation, and lightness approach so that the new colors are visually plausible, with an optional seed so results can be reproduced. Allow the user to control how much the colors change, and make it possible to exclude specific colors from being altered. The output should use colored terminal text for readability when the terminal supports it, and the script should exit with a clear status code indicating success, nothing found, or an error. Include a command-line interface with helpful usage text, and make sure file write operations are safe, such as writing through a temporary file so a failed write never corrupts the original. ---

comment_out.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for commenting out a specified range of lines in a source file. The tool should accept three arguments: the path to a file, a starting line number, and an ending line number. It must validate its inputs and exit with a clear error message when arguments are missing, when line numbers are not valid integers, when line numbers are out of order or less than 1, or when the file does not exist. Once the inputs are validated, the tool should determine the correct single-line comment syntax based on the file's extension, supporting common languages such as Python, shell scripts, YAML, Ruby, JavaScript, TypeScript, C, C++, Java, and Go, and falling back to a hash-style comment for unrecognized extensions. Each line within the requested inclusive range should be prefixed with the appropriate comment marker while preserving the original indentation and the rest of the line content. The modified content should be written back to the same file, and the tool should report a concise success message indicating how many lines were commented. For HTML and CSS files, the tool should handle their comment conventions appropriately so that the resulting file remains syntactically valid. The tool should be robust to files with varying encodings where reasonable, avoid altering lines outside the requested range, and keep the implementation clean, readable, and easy to run from a terminal. ---

compare_files_dirs.py: Write a Python script that compares two file system locations (individual files or directory trees) and reports how they differ, supporting both a quick check and a detailed content-level comparison. The script should accept two paths as command-line inputs, expand environment variables and user home shorthands, and resolve them to absolute locations before comparing. When both inputs are files, it should determine whether they are identical and, if they differ, show a unified-style textual diff of their contents, handling text files with a configurable or automatically detected encoding and gracefully falling back when a file cannot be read as text. When both inputs are directories, it should walk the full tree recursively, identify files present only on one side, files present on both sides with differing content, and files that match, and report these categories clearly. Content comparison should be based on a cryptographic checksum computed inamed chunks so that very large files can be handled without excessive memory use, with a fast metadata-based pre-check available as an optional shortcut. The script should support options that allow the user to control the output: a summary-only mode, a verbose mode that prints per-file details, a mode that shows diffs for changed text a configurable number of contextit or exclude certain paths or file patterns. It may optionally synchronize or copy differences from one side to the other, but only when explicitly requested by a flag, and it should require confirmation or a dry-run preview before making any changes. Output should be human-readable by default, with clear section headers and counts of identical, changed, and unique files, and it should exit with a non-zero status code when differences are found so it can be used in scripts and CI pipelines. Errors such as missing paths, permission problems, or unreadable files should be reported to the user without crashing the entire run, and the script should provide helpful usage text. Optional colored terminal output should be used if a styling helper is available, falling back to plain printing otherwise. ---

compile_c_cpp_files.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans the current working directory for C and C++ source files (.c and .cpp), compiles each one in parallel using an external compiler command supplied to the program, and reports the outcome of every compilation. The script should: - Accept the compiler to use (for example gcc, g++, clang, or clang++) as an input, choosing an appropriate compiler for each source type when a sensible default is available, while allowing the user to override it. - Search all subdirectories of the starting directory, collecting every C source file and every C++ source file it finds. - Produce an executable for each source file, named after the source file without its extension and placed alongside it in the same directory. - Run the compilations concurrently across multiple worker processes to take advantage of available CPU cores, with a reasonable upper bound on the number of workers. - Enforce a per-file time limit so that a hanging compilation is terminated and reported as a timeout rather than blocking the whole run. - Capture compiler diagnostics so that failures display the relevant error output to the user. - Print a live or summarized status line for each file as it finishes, using clear success and failure markers, and print the scanned root directory at the start. - Handle unexpected errors for individual files gracefully so that one failure never stops the remaining compilations. - Finish with a summary showing how many files compiled successfully and how many failed, and exit with a non-zero status code if any compilation failed. - Be runnable as a standalone command-line program with a main entry point, and include brief usage guidance for the user. ---

compile_precise2.py: Write a Python script that builds a print-ready CSS stylesheet with embedded typefaces for PDF generation. The script should look for a set of local font files in the current working directory (a regular, bold, italic, and bold-italic variant of a sans-serif family such as Inter, plus a monospace font such as JetBrains Mono). For each font file found, it should read the binary contents and embed them directly into the stylesheet as base64-encoded data so the output is fully self-contained and portable. If any font file is missing, the script should print a clear warning to the console explaining that the rendering engine will fall back to default system typography for that style, and continue without failing. The script should print progress messages to the console as it works, such as indicating when it begins parsing the typography files. Its final output is a complete CSS string containing the generated font-face declarations followed by a set of precise, professional styling rules intended for an HTML-to-PDF rendering pipeline (for example, WeasyPrint). The styling should cover base body typography, headings at multiple levels, paragraphs, lists, code blocks and inline code using the monospace font, tables, blockquotes, links, and page-level print settings such as page size, margins, and page numbering in headers or footers. The design should emphasize clean hierarchy, comfortable line height, readable font sizes, and consistent spacing suitable for formal documents. The script should be designed to be imported as a module or run directly, with the CSS-building function returning the stylesheet string so that other tools can consume it. Handle file-reading errors gracefully, keep the font-loading logic robust when only some fensure the generated CSS remains valid even if no fonts are found at all (in which case only the non-font styling rules are emitted). ---

compress_subdirs.py: Write a Python script that creates compressed archives of one or more files or directories, supporting multiple compression formats (xz, gzip, bzip2, zstandard, and lz4) selectable from the command line. The tool should accept one or more source paths and an output location, package the contents into a single tar-based archive, and compress it using the chosen algorithm, automatically appending the standard file extension for that format. It should allow the user to pick the compression method, and optionally adjust the compression level or preset where the format supports it, favoring maximum compression by default. Where practical, it should use parallelism to speed up compression of large inputs, and it should handle missing paths, unsupported formats, and existing output files gracefully with clear error messages and sensible exit codes. The script should report progress or a summary of what was archived, including the output file path and resulting size, and it should clean up partial output if an operation fails. Ensure that optional dependencies (such as the lz4 library) are only required when that format is selected, and provide helpful guidance if they are missing. Include a clear command-line interface with help text, and make the tool work reliably across major operating systems. ---

compress_text.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line archive compressor and benchmarking tool. It should accept one or more input files or directories, compress them using several selectable compression algorithms (such as gzip-style, bzip2, LZMA/XZ, Brotli, PPMd, and Zstandard-style codecs where available), and produce compressed output files or a single archive. The tool should be able to run multiple compression jobs in parallel across CPU cores, with a configurable worker count, and it should show a live, visually rich terminal dashboard with per-task progress bars, transfer speeds, elapsed time, and an overall summary table at the end. Key behaviors: - Accept command-line arguments for input paths, output location, the list of algorithms to try, compression level or preset (including an "extreme" mode), chunk and buffer sizing, and the number of parallel workers. - Support a mode that compresses each input with every requested algorithm and reports a comparison table of original size, compressed size, compression ratio, and time taken, ranking the results. - Handle directories by recursively collecting files and preserving their relative structure, optionally packing them into a tar stream before compression. - Verify integrity: after compression, optionally decompress in memory or to a temporary location and compare checksums (such as SHA-256) against the original, reporting any mismatch clearly. - Write a small self-describing header or metadata record alongside compressed payloads (for example, the algorithm name, original size, and checksum) so that the output can be identified and validated later, and provide a matching decompression/inspection mode. - Communicate between worker processes and the main process through a queue so progress updates flow to the dashboard in real time without blocking the workers; report and recover gracefully from worker errors, printing full tracebacks in a dedicated error panel without crashing the whole run. - Optionally export the final results as a JSON report file. - Skip codecs whose optional third-party dependencies are not installed, warn the user about them, and continue with the remaining algorithms. - Handle keyboard interrupts cleanly by cancelling pending jobs, terminating workers, removing partial output files, and printing a summary of what completed. - Show clear, friendly usage help and validate all user input with informative error messages before any work begins. ---

compression_benchmark.py: Write a Python script that acts as a universal file compression benchmarking and conversion tool. The script should take a source file path as input and compress it using a wide range of compression algorithms and archive formats, including common ones (gzip, bzip2, LZMA/XZ, ZIP, TAR-based archives) and optional third-party codecs (such as Brotli, ZZ4, 7z, LZMA-alone, Zopfli-optimized gzip, PPMd, Deflate64, and encrypted ZIP variants). Each compressor should be exposed as a pluggable, named option that takes an input file, an output location, and an optional compression level, and returns the result of the operation. The tool should gracefully handle missing optional dependencies: any codec whose library is not installed should be skipped or reported as unavailable rather than causing the script to crash, and the user should be informed which formats are supported in the current environment. Key behaviors: - Accept a file path (and optionally a list of algorithms or a "run all" mode) from the command line. - For each selected algorithm, compress the input into a temporary or designated output location, using a configurable compression level where the codec supports one. - Measure and report, for each algorithm, the compressed size, compression ratio versus the original, elapsed compression time, and whether the operation succeeded or failed. - Optionally verify each output by decompressing it and comparing the result to the original bytes, reporting any mismatch. - Clean up temporary files and handle errors per algorithm so that one failing codec does not stop the others. - Present results in a clear, sorted summary table (e.g., by size or by time), and optionally export the results to a machine-readable format such as JSON or CSV. - Provide helpful error messages for invalid paths, unsupported options, or missing dependencies, and exit with an appropriate status code. The script should be self-contained, well-organized, and designed so that new compression backends can be added easily by registering them alongside the existing ones. ---

compresstools.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line batch compression tool for files and directories. The tool should accept a target path (a single file or a folder) and an algorithm choice, then compress the contents using one of several widely used formats, including Zstandard, XZ, 7z, Gzip, Bzip2, Brotli, and LZ4. Each format should use sensible high-compression defaults that can be tuned. The script should walk through the specified folder (optionally recursing into subfolders), process multiple files concurrently with a bounded number of worker threads or tasks, and write each output archive or compressed file alongside the original with the correct extension for its format. It should also support an option to bundle a whole directory into a single compressed tarball (e.g., .tar.zst or .tar.xz) rather than compressing each file individually. Key behaviors to include: - Report progress and a final summary showing how many files were processed, skipped, or failed, along with the original and compressed sizes and the overall compression ratio, using human-readable size formatting. - Skip files that are already compressed or that have already been processed, unless an overwrite flag is given. - Detect and gracefully handle missing optional compression libraries, marking those formats as unavailable instead of crashing, and list which formats are available when requested. - Provide a dry-run mode that reports what would be done without writing any files. - Handle errors per file without stopping the whole batch, and return a non-zero exit status if any failures occurred. - Validate inputs with clear error messages for invalid paths or unsupported algorithms. - Use a clean command-line interface with help text, and read compression chunk sizes in reasonably large blocks for efficient streaming of large files. ---

comprust.py: Write a Python script that takes a text file path from the command line, reads the file's contents, runs them through a text compression routine that shortens the text while preserving its meaning, and saves the compressed result to a new file placed alongside the original, using the same base name with a distinct ".compressed" extension. The script should be runnable directly from the terminal, accept the target file as its single argument, and rely on an external compression component to perform the actual compression, returning the compressed text as its output. Keep the workflow simple and self-contained: one file in, one compressed file out, with the original file left unchanged. ---

compy.py: Write a Python script that acts as a source-code compressor for Python files. It should take one or more Python source files (or a directory tree of them) as input and produce a minified, condensed version of the code intended to reduce size while preserving exact runtime behavior. The tool should work in parallel across multiple files to speed up processing, and write its combined compressed output to a single text file in the current working directory. Key behaviors to implement: - Remove comments, docstrings, shebang lines, and unnecessary whitespace and blank lines, while keeping the code syntactically valid and functionally identical. - Rename local identifiers (variables, function parameters, and user-defined names inside scopes) to short generated names to shrink the output, but never rename Python keywords, built-in names, module-level public APIs, attribute names accessed on external objects, or a configurable set of protected dunder and conventional names (such as `self`, `cls`, `__init__`, `__name__`, and similar special methods and attributes). - Preserve string literals and f-string semantics exactly; do not alter their contents. - Handle imports correctly so that names used from imported modules are not renamed and the code still runs. - Verify that each compressed output still parses as valid Python; if a transformation would break a file, fall back to a safer, less aggressive compression for that file and report it. - Provide a command-line interface with arguments to specify input paths, output file location, number of worker processes, and options to toggle individual compression stages (comment stripping, renaming, whitespace collapsing). - Print a concise summary at the end showing the number of files processed, original versus compressed size in bytes, and the percentage reduction achieved, along with any files that fell back or failed. - Handle errors gracefully (unreadable files, syntax errors in input, encoding issues) by logging the problem and continuing with the remaining files rather than aborting the whole run. ---

compy2.py: Write a Python script that acts as a source-code compressor for Python projects. It should take a Python source file (or a directory of Python files) as input and produce a single, reduced output file that is functionally equivalent but substantially smaller in size. The tool should be designed to run its per-file work in parallel across multiple worker processes to speed up processing of large codebases. Key behaviors to implement: - Accept input via command-line arguments, including the path to the source to compress and an optional output path, with a sensible default output filename when none is given. - Parse each Python file structurally so that transformations are safe: strip comments and unnecessary whitespace, remove docstrings where they are not needed for runtime behavior, and consolidate formatting while preserving valid syntax. - Remove imports of standard library modules from the compressed output, while keeping any third-party or project-local dependencies intact, and prepend a clear note in the output explaining that the code has been compressed and that standard library imports were removed. - Shorten local identifiers (variables, functions, and parameters) to short generated names to reduce size, but never rename names that are Python keywords, built-in names, dunder/protected special methods and attributes, `self`/`cls`, module-level public API names that must remain stable, or names that are accessed dynamically through strings. Maintain consistent renaming within each scope so that the code still runs identically. - Avoid collisions when generating short names, and ensure the set of generated names does not clash with existing identifiers or reserved words. - Use a protected-names list and a builtins-aware check so that the renaming logic is conservative and safe rather than aggressive. - Process multiple files concurrently using a configurable number of worker processes (defaulting to a modest number such as eight), and merge or write results deterministically. - Report progress and a summary at the end, including original versus compressed size and the percentage reduction. - Handle errors gracefully: skip or report files that fail to parse, and never silently produce corrupted output. Validate that the compressed output is syntactically valid Python before writing it. - Keep the overall tool self-contained, readable, and robust, with clear usage help available through the command line. ---

consolidate.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for splitting a single merged Python source file into multiple separate module files, and conversely understands and processes files that were previously merged together with per-file header comments. The tool should take a merged Python file as input (and an output directory or destination as a second input), detect the logical sections of the merged file based on embedded "# File: <path>" markers, and recreate the original project structure by writing each section to its corresponding path with proper relative layout.
