Key behaviors: - Resume interrupted downloads from partial files on disk without re-fetching completed data, and never corrupt an existing finished file unless explicitly told to overwrite it. - Retry failed segments or requests with backoff, handling network errors, timeouts, and transient HTTP errors gracefully, while reporting permanent failures clearly. - Display a live progress indicator per file showing bytes transferred, percentage, speed, and estimated time remaining, and print a concise summary at the end. - Verify integrity by computing a hash (such as MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256) of the completed file and comparing it against an expected value when provided, reporting mismatches. - Handle user interruption (such as Ctrl+C) cleanly by saving progress so the transfer can be resumed later, without leaving corrupted output. - Sanitize output filenames derived from URLs, avoid overwriting unrelated files, and create the output directory if needed. - Optionally use multiple worker processes or threads to download several files concurrently, with a configurable limit. - Log activity to both the console and an optional log file at a configurable verbosity level. - Exit with a meaningful status code: zero when all downloads succeed and verify, non-zero otherwise. Use only standard practices suitable for a robust, production-quality command-line utility, and provide clear help text describing all options. ---

dll.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line utility for removing a range of lines from a text file in place. The script should accept a file path as its first argument, followed by a starting line number and an optional ending line number. When only a starting line is given, all lines from that position to the end of the file should be removed. When both a start and end line are given, the lines in that inclusive range should be removed, with the line numbering following a 1-based convention. The script should read the file using UTF-8 encoding, perform the deletion, overwrite the original file with the remaining content, and print a short message reporting how many lines remain. Handle the input as simply as possible from the command line, and assume the user supplies valid arguments. Keep the tool focused, self-contained, and easy to run directly from a terminal. ---

docer.py: Write a Python script that takes a single file path from the command line, moves that file into a fixed destination folder used for storing documents on an Android device (under /sdcard/doc), and reports the outcome to the user. The script should create the destination folder if it does not already exist. If a file with the same name is already present in the destination, the script must leave both the source and the existing destination file untouched and print a clear message telling the user the target file already exists and that they should remove it and try again. Otherwise, the script should copy the file's contents into the destination, delete the original source file so the move is complete, and print a short confirmation that the operation finished. The script should run as a standalone command-line tool, read its input from the first command-line argument, and perform the operation without any interactive prompts. ---

docstring_formatter.py: Write a Python script that analyzes the source code of other Python files and reformats their docstrings and long comment or text blocks to improve readability. The tool should accept a file or directory path as input, walk through Python source files while skipping common non-source or virtual environment directories (such as version control folders, caches, build outputs, and dependency folders), and locate string literals that serve as docstrings. For each docstring, it should normalize the text by re-wrapping prose so that lines do not exceed a configurable maximum width (default 80 characters), while preserving the original meaning, paragraph breaks, and the indentation level of the enclosing code. It should recognize and keep intact list items (numbered, bulleted, or bold-labeled entries) by placing them on their own lines, and avoid altering code examples or content that must remain verbatim. The tool must preserve the file's string prefixes, quote styles, and triple-quote delimiters, and must ensure the rewritten file still parses as valid Python. It should support a dry-run mode that reports which files and docstrings would change without writing anything, a mode that writes changes in place, and a summary output listing the number of files scanned, files modified, and docstrings reformatted. Handle encoding errors, unreadable files, and syntax errors gracefully by logging a warning and continuing with the remaining files. Exit with a non-zero status if any file could not be processed, and zero otherwise. ---

doctools.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line utility for organizing and exporting files from a local directory tree, with a set of subcommands selected via command-line arguments. The tool should accept an input path (a file or a directory) and an output location, and should be able to filter files by extension, optionally recursing into subdirectories. It should handle chat-export style text or JSON files as a primary use case: read an exported conversation file, validate that it exists and is well-formed, and convert it into a cleaner, normalized output format such as Markdown or plain text, with a clear per-message structure including speaker, timestamp when tool should also provide supporting file-management behaviors: when a destination file already exists, it must never silently overwrite it and should instead generate a unique non-conflicting name. It should log progress messages to the console with clear informational, warning, and error levels, sending warnings and errors to the error stream while keeping informational output on the standard stream. Errors such as missing input files should produce a clear message and a non-zero exit status rather than an unhandled crash. Where batch processing is involved, the tool should be able to process many files efficiently, optionally in parallel across multiple worker processes, and should report a summary of successes, skips, and failures at the end. It should compute and optionally report content fingerprints for files so that duplicates can be identified. Where external tooling is needed (for example, to inspect or convert media or archives), the script should check that the required system command is available and fail gracefully with a helpful message if it is not. The script should be invoked with clearly named subcommands and standard help text, validate all arguments before doing work, and be structured so that each subcommand is independently testable. It should run as a standalone script with a conventional entry point and return a meaningful process exit code. ---

dostounix.py: Write a Python script that converts text files from Windows-style line endings (CRLF) to Unix-style line endings (LF), operating on files supplied as command-line arguments. Each argument may be either a file or a directory; when a directory is given, the script should recursively process all files within it. If no arguments are provided, the script should default to processing the current working directory recursively. The tool should: - Accept one or more file directory paths as input, expanding user home shortcuts and resolving them to absolute paths. - Automatically skip binary files and any files matching a project-defined exclusion rule, so that only plain text files are considered. - Detect whether each file contains CRLF line endings. Files without CRLF should be left untouched and reported as unchanged. - For files containing CRLF sequences, replace every CRLF with LF and write the result back to the original file. The conversion should be safe: write through a temporary file and atomically replace the original so that a failed write never leaves a corrupted or partially written file. - Process files in parallel using a pool of worker processes (around 8 workers) with batched task distribution for efficiency. - Handle file system errors such as permission problems or read/write failures gracefully: record the error for the affected file, continue processing the remaining files, and never crash the whole run because of a single file. - Report a summary at the end, including the number of files scanned, the number converted, the number skipped as unchanged, and a list of any files that failed with their error messages. Output should be clear, concise, and suitable for terminal use. - Exit with a non-zero status code if any file failed to convert, and zero otherwise. Keep the implementation self-contained in a single script with a clear `main` entry point, and ensure it is safe to run on large directory trees. ---

dostring_browser.py: Write a Python script that acts as an interactive terminal viewer for Markdown documents. The tool should accept one or more Markdown file paths from the command line and render them with rich formatting in the terminal, one "page" of content at a time, so the user can read long documents comfortably without leaving the console. Core behavior: - Take a list of Markdown files as input; if none are given, the tool should report a clear usage error or display a helpful message instead of failing silently. - Split each document into screen-sized pages based on the current terminal dimensions, so that content fits the visible area and can be paged through naturally. - Present rendered Markdown (headings, lists, code blocks, emphasis, tables, and similar elements) with attractive, readable styling in the terminal. - Provide keyboard-driven navigation: advance and go back by page, jump to the first or last page, move between multiple files in the order they were supplied, and quit at any time using common quit keys. Support a range of familiar key bindings (including arrow keys, space, and vim-style letters) where the environment allows, and degrade gracefully to simple line-based input when raw keyboard reading is unavailable. - Display a status indicator showing the current file name, page position, and navigation hints. - Handle edge cases robustly: missing or unreadable files, empty documents, very small terminals, and unexpected key presses should not crash the program. Exit cleanly and restore the terminal state on quit or interruption. - Keep the user experience responsive and the terminal output clean, with no leftover artifacts after exiting. The script should be a single self-contained command-line utility that prioritizes a smooth, distraction-free reading experience. ---

drmc.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for stripping comments and docstrings from Python source files in a project, while keeping the code valid and runnable. The tool should accept one or more file or directory paths, recursively discover Python files (skipping common cache, version-control, virtual-environment, and build-artifact directories), and process them in parallel for speed. For each file, it should read the source using several fallback text encodings, remove comments and docstrings safely (preserving code structure and any content that must remain, such as the shebang line and encoding declarations), and verify that the resulting code still parses correctly before writing anything. The tool should support a dry-run mode that reports what would change, including a colored, human-readable diff and per-file statistics such as bytes removed, comments removed, and docstrings removed, without modifying files. It should also offer an option to create backups or write results to an output location, and it should produce a concise summary at the end with totals, the number of files changed, errors encountered, and elapsed time. Errors on individual files must not stop the overall run; they should be logged clearly and reported in the summary. Logging should use a structured logging library, and the command-line interface should provide clear help text and a non-zero exit status when failures occur. ---

dt1.py: Write a Python script that translates the text content of a file (or multiple files) from one language to another, using a chain of fallback translation services so that if one service fails or is rate-limited, the next one is tried automatically. The tool should be a command-line application that accepts input file paths, a target language (with a source language that defaults to automatic detection), and options controlling output location, concurrency, and request pacing to avoid overloading translation services. Language identifiers should be normalized through common aliases (for example, mapping variant spellings of Chinese or Portuguese codes to their standard forms). Key behaviors: - Read the input text, split it into manageable chunks that respect service length limits, translate the chunks, and reassemble them so that the original structure, line breaks, and formatting are preserved as closely as possible. - Attempt translation through an ordered list of backend services (such as DeepL, deep_translator, translate, Bing via translators, googletrans, and pygoogletranslation), moving to the next backend when one fails, times out, or returns an error. Raise a clear error only when all backends have failed. - Enforce a configurable delay between outgoing requests in a thread-safe way, so that parallel workers do not exceed the request rate. - Support parallel translation of chunks using a configurable number of worker threads, with results collected in the correct original order. - Write the translated output to a file, using a sensible default naming scheme that includes the target language, and never overwrite the original input unless explicitly allowed. Write output atomically (for example, through a temporary file and rename) to avoid corrupted results on interruption. - Log progress, warnings about backend failures, and final statistics using a structured logging approach, with verbosity controlled from the command line. - Handle keyboard interruption gracefully by cancelling pending work and reporting what was completed. - Provide helpful error messages for missing files, unsupported languages, invalid arguments, and empty input, and exit with appropriate non-zero status codes on failure. - Accept an option to dry-run or preview the chunking plan without calling any translation service. ---

dt2.py: Write a Python script that translates a large text file containing many lines (for example, a list of phrases or sentences) into a target language using an online machine translation service, with the goal of producing a translated output file that preserves line-by-line correspondence with the original. The tool should accept command-line arguments for the input file path, the output file path, the source and target languages, and optional settings controlling concurrency and chunk sizing. It should split the input into manageable batches, translate them in parallel across multiple worker processes or threads, and retry failed requests with a delay between attempts. Long lines that exceed the batch size limit should be handled gracefully by translating them individually or by splitting them into smaller pieces and rejoining the results. Include a feature that detects whether the translated output still contains untranslated text in a specific script (such as Cyrillic characters) and flags or re-translates those lines accordingly. The script should periodically save progress so that an interrupted run can resume without re-translating completed lines, and it should respond to a keyboard interrupt by saving current progress and exiting cleanly. Log progress, warnings, and errors to both the console and a log file, and display a summary at the end reporting how many lines were translated, skipped, retried, or failed. Preserve empty lines and the original line count in the output, and write the results in UTF-8 encoding. ---

dt3.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line batch translation tool for text files. It should accept an input file path, a source language (defaulting to automatic detection), a target language, and an output path, then translate the file's contents and save the result. The tool should support a predefined set of common language codes (including regional variants such as Brazilian Portuguese and Simplified Chinese, with sensible mappings between user-facing codes and the codes expected by the translation backend). It should allow the user to choose among multiple translation backends through a plugin-style mechanism, so that new providers can be added without changing the core logic, and it should ship with at least one default backend that requires no API key. Key behaviors to include: - Split long input into manageable chunks that respect sentence or line boundaries, translate them concurrently with a configurable number of worker threads, and reassemble them in their original order. - Show progress as chunks complete, and log useful information (timing, chunk counts, errors) using a logging facility. - Retry failed translation requests with a configurable number of attempts and backoff, and fail gracefully with a clear message if a chunk cannot be translated. - Preserve line breaks and basic formatting structure of the original document where possible. - Optionally use a translation memory or cache so that repeated sentences are not re-translated within or across runs, and optionally compare results against a reference file to report a similarity score using a fuzzy text-matching measure. - Write output atomically (to a temporary file first, then move it into place) so a partial run never corrupts the destination file. - Accept a command-line flag toported languages and backends, and validate all user inputs with helpful error messages before doing any work. - Load any custom backend or plugin module from a user-specified path at runtime. - Exit with meaningful non-zero status codes on failure, and print a concise summary of the run (characters processed, chunks translated, elapsed time) on success. ---

dt4.py: Write a Python script that translates a large text file from one language to another, using a free online translation service, and saves the results as structured JSON chunks. The tool should read an input text file, split its content into manageable chunks of a configurable size (preferably breaking at natural boundaries such as sentences or paragraphs), and translate each chunk independently. It should accept command-line arguments for the input file, output file, failed-items file, source and target language codes, number of concurrent workers, delay between requests, chunk size, and how often progress is saved. Key behaviors: - Translate chunks concurrently with a configurable number of workers, while respecting a small delay between requests to avoid rate limiting. - Map common ISO language codes (such as en, fr, es, de, it, pt, ru, zh, ja, ar) to the naming conventions expected by the translation backend, and reject unsupported codes with a clear error. - Retry failed translations with exponential backoff up to a fixed maximum number of attempts, and distinguish between transient errors (which should be retried) and permanent ones (which should be recorded and skipped). - Periodically save progress so that an interrupted run can resume without re-translating already completed chunks. - Write successfully translated chunks to the output JSON file, preserving their original order and including both source and translated text along with identifiers. - Record any chunks that could not be translated into a separate failed-items file so the user can review or retry them later. - Handle keyboard interruption (Ctrl+C) gracefully by saving current progress before exiting. - Log progress, warnings, and errors to the console with clear, readable messages, and print a final summary of successes, failures, and elapsed time. - Validate inputs up front (file existence, valid language codes, positive numeric parameters) and report problems with helpful messages instead of crashing. ---

dt5.py: Write a Python script that acts as a batch translation tool for text and structured files, built around a pluggable set of translation backends with configurable language mappings. The tool should accept command-line arguments specifying the input source, target language(s), source language (optionally auto-detected), the translation provider to use, and an output location, and it should process the input concurrently to speed up large batches while respecting rate limits and remaining responsive to interruption signals (such as Ctrl+C), shutting down gracefully and reporting partial progress. Key behaviors to include: - Support multiple translation providers, each with its own mapping from common language codes to the codes that provider expects, and fall back gracefully or report clearly when a language is unsupported by the chosen provider. - Accept input as individual strings, plain text files, or structured data files, and produce output that preserves the original structure and formatting of the input as closely as possible. - Run translation jobs in parallel with a configurable number of workers, retry transient failures with backoff, and track progress so the user can see how many items have completed, failed, or been skipped. - Allow the user to resume an interrupted run by reusing previously completed results stored in an intermediate or cache file, avoiding duplicate API calls. - Provide clear logging: a detailed debug log written to a rotating file, and only error-level messages echoed to the console. - Validate all arguments up front, with helpful error messages for missing API keys, unsupported language pairs, unreadable input files, or unwritable output paths. - Produce a concise final summary on completion (total items, successes, failures, elapsed time) and exit with a meaningful status code reflecting success, partial failure, or fatal error. The script should be self-contained, runnable from the command line, and well-organized so that adding a new translation provider requires minimal changes. ---

dtg.py: Write a Python script that scans a Python source file and translates its human-readable text into another language while leaving the code's logic untouched. The tool should accept a source file path, a target language, and optional settings such as an output path, a model or service to use for translation, and the level of parallelism. It should identify which text is meant for people rather than the computer: string literals passed to output functions (such as printing messages), docstrings for modules, classes, and functions, and comments. Everything else, including identifiers, control flow, imports, and non-human-facing string values, must be preserved exactly as written. The script should parse the source so that it understands the structure of the code, then extract the translatable segments along with their precise locations. It should send those segments for translation in batches or concurrently to improve throughput, handle transient failures with retries and backoff, and respect rate limits. Progress should be tracked in a small state file so that an interrupted run can resume without re-translating completed segments, and a changed source should invalidate only the affected entries. Once translation is complete, the script should write a new Python file that reproduces the original code with the translated text substituted in place, preserving indentation, quoting style, string prefixes (such as raw or byte markers), triple-quoted formatting, and comment markers. The output must remain valid, runnable Python, and the script should verify this before reporting success, falling back to the original text for any segment that fails to translate or would break syntax. It should also provide a concise summary at the end covering how many segments were translated, skipped, cached from a previous run, and failed, and it should exit with a non-zero status code when errors prevent a complete result. Include clear command-line help, sensible defaults, and informative logging so that a user can follow the progress of a long run on a large project. ---

dtluna.py: Write a Python script that acts as a multi-engine text translation tool with a command-line interface. It should accept source and target language codes (with "auto" detection for the source), take input text from a file or direct argument, and produce translated output written to a file or standard output. The tool should support several translation backends, allowing the user to choose one, and should use a fallback strategy so that if one backend fails or is unavailable, another can be tried. It should translate in parallel batches for efficiency, preserve the original line or paragraph structure of the input, and report progress and errors through a logging facility. Include a quality or similarity check that compares results from multiple engines and selects or flags the most consistent translation. The tool should handle common language code aliases (such as Chinese variants and Portuguese Brazilian), validate unsupported codes with a clear error message, support retries with backoff for transient network failures, and optionally load custom translator plugins from a user-provided Python module path. Provide a summary of results at the end, including counts of successes, failures, and the backend used for each segment. ---

dup_detector.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory t detects duplicate oritions across them, so a developer can find copy-pasted logic that should be consolidated. The tool should accept a root directory path as its main input, along with optional settings such as a similarity threshold for flagging near forects worurse through all subdirectories, skip a conventional and opping the overall run. From each readable file, the script should identify top-level functions, async functions, and classes, and capture each one's name, source location, and normalized body text. Trivial objects below the size threshold should be excluded from comparison. The core behavior is to compare objects pairwise across files and report two categories of matches: exact duplicates (identical content after normalization,espace and comments differences where feasible) and near-duplicates whose fuzzy similarity score meets or exceeds the configured threshold. Choose a sensible, efficient strategy so that large codebases remain tractable, for example by grouping candidates with cheap fingerprints before doing expensive similarity checks, and consider using parallel processing where it helps. The output should be a structured report, available as human-readable text on the console and optionally as machine-readable JSON written to a file. Each finding should list the matching objects with their file paths, line ranges, object types, and the similarity score. Results should be sorted so the most significant duplicates appear first, and the script should print a concise summary of total files scanned, objects analyzed, and duplicate groups found. The script should handle missing optional dependencies gracefully by printing a clear installation message and exiting with a non-zero status. It should provide a command-line interface with helpful usage text, validate its inputs, and exit with appropriate status codes for success, invalid arguments, and runtime errors. ---

dupdirs.py: Write a Python script that scans one or more directory trees and reports groups of duplicate files based on content. The tool should accept a root directory path from the command line, walk through its subdirectories while ignoring version-control metadata folders (such as `.git`), and avoid following symbolic links. It should guard against excessively deep directory nesting and tolerate unreadable directories or files without crashing. For each regular file found, the script should compute a fast, non-cryptographic content fingerprint by reading the file in fixed-size chunks so that large files do not exhaust memory. Files should first be grouped by size so that only candidates with identical sizes are fimizing unnecessary disk reads. The fingerprinting work should be parallelized across multiple worker processes to speed up scanning of large trees. The final output should list every set of two or more files that have identical content, showing each group's file size and the paths of its members, ordered in a readable way (for example, largest groups or largest files first). Optionally, the tool should support a summary mode that reports the total number of duplicate files and the reclaimable disk space. Provide clear command-line options for the root path, worker count, and output format, with helpful usage messages and graceful handling of errors such as missing paths or permission problems. Exit with a non-zero status code on fatal errors and zero otherwise. ---

dupeguru.py: Write a Python script that scans one or more user-specified directory trees and identifies groups of duplicate files, so the user can review and reclaim wasted disk space. The tool should accept one or more root folders from the command line, along with optional settings such as minimum file size, directories to exclude, and whether to follow symbolic links (off by default). It should recursively traverse the given locations, skipping common non-user directories such as version control metadata, dependency caches, build output, IDE settings, and OS trash or system folders, while handling unreadable paths and permission errors gracefully without crashing. To keep the process efficient, the script should first group candidate files by size, discarding files that have a unique size, and then narrow matches by comparing a small leading sample of each file before performing a full content comparison on the remaining candidates. Content comparison should use a cryptographic hash computed in streamed chunks so that large files never need to be loaded into memory at once. The script should make use of parallel processing where it meaningfully speeds up hashing of many files, while remaining safe across platforms. The output should be a human-readable report listing each set of identical files with their shared size, the paths belonging to each group, and a summary of the total number of duplicate groups, duplicate files, and the reclaimable disk space in a readable unit format (such as KiB, MiB, or GiB). The script should optionally export the same results in a machine-readable format such as JSON or CSV. It must never delete, move, or modify any files on its own; it should only report findings, and it should exit with a clear status code indicating success, invalid arguments, or errors encountered during the scan. ---

dupeguru_textual.py: Write a Python script that provides an interactive terminal-based tool for finding and managing duplicate files within one or more chosen directories. The tool should present a full-screen text user interface where the user can browse a directory tree, select folders to scan, and launch a scan that walks the selected locations and collects file metadata such as path, size, and modification details. The scan should identify duplicates in two ways: exact duplicates, where files have identical contents (confirmed by comparing content fingerprints, with size used as a fast pre-filter), and near-duplicates, where file names are highly similar (for example, the same base name with different casing, spacing, or numbered suffixes like "copy" or "(1)"), scored by a similarity percentage against a configurable threshold. Each detected group should record why it was matched and a match score. The interface should show progress during scanning, list the duplicate groups in a sortable table, and let the user inspect the files within a group. For each group, the user should be able to choose which copy to keep, with a sensible default (such as keeping the oldest or shortest-path file), and then delete the others or move them to a holding folder. Provide a summary of how many files and how much disk space would be or was reclaimed. Destructive actions must require explicit confirmation in a modal dialog, and a dry-run mode should be available that reports planned actions without changing anything. The tool should also allow the user to adjust settings through the interface, including the name-similarity threshold, whether to include hidden files, minimum file size to consider, and file extensions to include or exclude. Handle unreadable files, permission errors, and broken symbolic links gracefully by skipping them and reporting them in a log or status area rather than crashing. Keyboard shortcuts should be displayed in a footer, and the application should exit cleanly on request. ---

dupf.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree for duplicate files and reports groups of identical files. The tool should accept a root directory path from the command line and walk through all files beneath it, skipping symbolic links, empty files, unreadable or inaccessible files, and anything located inside common tooling or version-control directories such as version control metadata folders, Python bytecode caches, and linter or type-checker caches. For each remaining file, compute a fast, non-cryptographic content hash, streaming the file in fixed-size chunks so that large files do not exhaust memory. Hashing should be parallelized across multiple worker processes to speed up scanning of large trees, with a sensible default number of workers that the user can override from the command line. Files that cannot be read or hashed should be logged as warnings and excluded from results without stopping the overall run. Group files by their content hash and identify every group containing two or more files as duplicates. The output should list each duplicate group clearly, showing the shared hash and the full paths of all files in that group, with groups ordered in a readable manner. Include a summary at the end reporting the total number of files scanned, the number of duplicate groups found, and the total number of redundant copies. Optionally, the tool should be able to report the total disk space that could be reclaimed by removing the redundant copies, using human-readable size formatting. Use proper structured logging for progress and diagnostic messages, keeping standard results separate from log output so the results can be redirected cleanly. Provide a clear command-line interface with helpful help text, sensible defaults, and input validation that exits with a meaningful error message when the provided path does not exist or is not a directory. The script should be runnable directly as a standalone program with a main entry point. ---

dupfuncanalyzer.py: Write a Python script that analyzes a collection of Python source files to detect functions that are duplicated across the codebase, and then produces a consolidated report or refactoring output identifying those repeated definitions. The tool should accept a directory (or set of files) as input, scan every Python file within it, and examine the top-level function definitions in each file. Two functions should be considered duplicates when their normalized source text matches, so the comparison should ignore insignificant differences such as leading/trailing whitespace and trailing spaces on lines. The analysis should track, for each unique function signature (name plus a definition identity), which files it appears in, and group together all occurrences that share identical implementations. Key behaviors: - Process files in parallel to handle large codebases efficiently, using a configurable worker pool with a sensible default size. - Read files as UTF-8, and gracefully skip or report files that cannot be read or parsed, without aborting the whole run. - Produce a single output file (with a configurable name and a sensible default) that lists each repeated function, the files where it occurs, and its source code, so a developer can review or consolidate it. - Optionally generate a shared module containing one canonical copy of each repeated function, and rewrite the original files so they import that canonical definition from a configurable module name instead of redefining it, while preserving the rest of each file's content. - Provide a command-line interface that lets the user specify the target path, output location, worker count, and whether to apply the consolidation. - Print a concise summary to the console indicating how many files were scanned, how many repeated functions were found, and where the report was written. - Handle edge cases such as no duplicates found, files with syntax errors, empty files, and non-Python content gracefully with clear messages. ---

dupfx.py: Write a Python script that finds duplicate files within one or more directories and reports them, so a user can review and clean up redundant copies. The tool should accept one or more directory paths from the command line, along with options that control behavior such as minimum file size, whether to recurse into subdirectories, and whether to include hidden files. It should walk the file tree and group candidate files that share the same size, since only files with identical sizes can be duplicates. For efficiency, it should first compare a small sample of each candidate (such as the beginning and end of the file) using a fast non-cryptographic hash, and only perform a full-content comparison on files that still match. Hard links to the same underlying file should be recognized and not reported as duplicates of each other. Use parallel processing to speed up hashing on large sets of files, with a sensible default number of workers that the user can adjust. Handle unreadable files, broken symlinks, permission errors, and files that disappear during the scan gracefully by logging a warning and continuing rather than aborting the whole run. The output should be a clear report listing each group of identical files, with their paths, sizes, and total reclaimable space. Support a machine-readable output option (such as JSON) in addition to a human-readable text summary. Optionally allow the user to write the report to a file instead of standard output. Use structured logging for progress and warnings, with a verbosity option that controls how much detail is shown. The script should exit with a zero status when the scan completes successfully and a non-zero status for invalid arguments or fatal errors. Include a command-line help message describing every option. ---

duptools.py: Write a Python script that scans one or more directory trees to find duplicate files and lets the user safely deduplicate them. The tool should work in a staged, progressively more expensive manner: first group files by size, then refine candidate groups using a cheap partial hash of the file head, then confirm true duplicates with a full-content hash, using multithreaded processing to keep scanning fast on large trees. Where optional high-performance or fuzzy-matching libraries are available, the script should make use of them, but it must still function fully using only the standard library. Key requirements: - **Inputs**: One or more root directories to scan, plus options for excluding directory names (with sensible default exclusions such as version control and cache folders), a worker count for parallelism, minimum file size thresholds, and an option to choose the hashing strategy or fuzzy/similarity mode. - **Outputs**: A human-readable report of duplicate groups (showing paths, sizes, and reclaimable space), and optionally a machine-readable JSON report. Progress feedback should be shown during long operations, with a graceful fallback when no progress-bar library is installed. - **Actions**: A dry-run mode that only reports what would change by default. When actions are enabled, the tool should be able to remove duplicates while keeping one canonical copy, or move duplicates into a stash directory instead of deleting them, so that the operation is reversible. Replacing duplicates with symbolic links to the kept copy should also be supported, with a manifest file recording every change so it can be audited or undone later. - **Safety**: Never act on files without explicit user intent; confirm or require a flag before destructive operations; handle permission errors, broken links, files disappearing mid-scan, and cross-device situations gracefully without crashing; avoid following symbolic links into unexpected locations during scanning. - **Behavior**: Deterministic choice of which copy to keep (for example, the first-encountered or shortest path), clear logging of each decision, a summary of total files scanned, groups found, and space that could be saved, and a non-zero exit code on fatal errors. - **Interface**: A clear command-line interface with help text, sensible defaults, and validation of arguments. ---

egg2whl.py: Write a Python script that converts an Python egg distribution (an unpacked `.egg` directory containing EGG-INFO metadata) into a buildable source project by reconstructing a `setup.py` file from the distribution's metadata. The script should take the path to the egg root directory as input and produce a ready-to-build setup script (written to a temporary or designated working location) that preserves the package name, version, and other core metadata read from the PKG-INFO file, along with any console or GUI entry points declared in an entry_points.txt file, and any dependency or package-data information available in the egg's metadata. Key requirements: - Read and parse the PKG-INFO metadata file tolerantly, handling non-UTF-8 bytes gracefully, and skip gracefully if the file is missing. - Generate a valid setuptools-based setup script that uses automatic package discovery, includes package data, and marks the package as not zip-safe. - Translate entry point definitions into the corresponding setup arguments, covering console scripts and other declared groups, and omit the entry point section cleanly when none exist. - Produce output in a temporary working directory that the user can inspect or build from, and clean up or report paths appropriately. - Optionally invoke the standard build tooling on the generated project when requested, reporting success or failure with clear messages. - Handle missing or malformed inputs with clear, user-friendly error messages rather than crashing unexpectedly. - Keep the script self-contained, command-line friendly, and well-structured with clear separation of parsing, generation, and output steps. ---

elf64.py: Write a Python script that scans a given directory tree for binary files and identifies 64-bit ELF executables and libraries, reporting each one's file type, target machine architecture, and size. The tool should accept a directory path from the command line, walk the directory recursively, and skip files that are not binary or cannot be read due to permission or I/O errors. For each qualifying file, it should determine the ELF file type (such as executable, shared object/PIE, relocatable object, or core dump) and the CPU architecture it targets (such as x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V, MIPS, PowerPC, and similar), falling back to a clear "unknown" label for unrecognized values. Malformed or non-ELF files should be silently ignored rather than crashing the run. Use parallel processing with a fixed pool of worker processes to speed up scanning of large trees. Collect the results and print them in a readable, aligned summary showing the path, file type, architecture, and size, followed by a total count of matching files. Include sensible error handling for an invalid or missing directory argument, and make sure the script exits with a non-zero status code on fatal errors and zero on success. ---

feloai.py: Write a Python script that acts as a logging wrapper around an external Node.js command-line tool. The script should accept arbitrary command-line arguments from the user, forward them unchanged to the external tool, run it as a subprocess, and faithfully relay its exit status. Every invocation must be recorded in a separate, uniquely named plain-text log file stored in a dedicated directory under the user's home folder (created automatically if it does not exist). Each log file should begin with a clear header containing the start timestamp, the current working directory, and the exact arguments that were passed, followed by a clearly marked output section where the tool's standard output and standard error are captured as they are produced. When the run finishes, the log should be closed with a footer that records the end timestamp and the process exit code. File names must be unique even when multiple runs occur within the same moment, using a timestamp-based naming scheme with a collision-avoidance suffix. The script should display the path of the log file it created so the user can find it, and should propagate the external tool's exit code as its own so it can be used reliably in shell scripts and pipelines. Handle common failure cases gracefully, such as the external tool being missing or not executable, by reporting a clear error message and returning a non-zero exit code. All text should be written and read using UTF-8 encoding. The script should target a Termux environment on Android but remain readable and maintainable, with the path to the external tool defined as a configurable constant at the top of the script. ---

felopy.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line wrapper around an external AI agent CLI. It should accept a free-form natural-language query from the user on the command line (multiple words joined together) along with an optional timeout setting in seconds, defaulting to five minutes. The script should forward the query to the external agent tool, wait for its response within the timeout, and report progress to the user on the standard error stream so that standard output stays clean. Once the agent returns its response, the script should scan the text for fenced code blocks, preferring blocks explicitly labeled as Python and falling back to unlabeled blocks if none are found. It should extract the code content from the first or most relevant block, strip surrounding whitespace, and save it as a Python file in a dedicated directory under the user's home folder, creating that directory if it does not exist. The filename should be generated automatically from a timestamp and a sanitized version of the query so that repeated runs never overwrite each other. The script should handle errors gracefully: report when the external tool is not installed or not found on the system path, report timeouts clearly, surface non-zero exit codes and error output from the external tool, and report when no code blocks are present in the response. On success, it should print the path of the saved file to the user. Keep the design simple, robust, and easy to run from a terminal, with a helpful usage message and description available through a help flag. ---

felormc.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for cleaning up and normalizing blank lines and related whitespace in Python source files, primarily around top-level and class-level definitions. The tool should accept one or more file or directory paths as input, recursively discover Python source files (recognizing standard Python extensions such as .py, .pyi, and .pyw, as well as extensionless scripts whose shebang line indicates a Python interpreter), and process them in parallel using a configurable number of worker processes with a sensible default. For each file, the script should parse the source into a concrete syntax tree that preserves comments, pragma directives (such as type-ignore, fmt-control, and noqa markers), and original formatting, then enforce consistent spacing rules: a standard number of blank lines between top-level function and class definitions, appropriate spacing for nested definitions, and no excessive blank lines at the start or end of blocks. It must leave pragma comments and shebang lines untouched in position and content, and must never alter the program's semantics. The tool should support a check mode that reports which files would change without modifying them, and a write mode that updates files in place. It should also support a verbose option that increases logging detail. Results for each file should be reported clearly, indicating whether the file was unchanged, reformatted, skipped, or failed due to a syntax error, and the overall run should summarize counts of each outcome. The script should exit with a non-zero status code when check mode finds files needing changes or when errors occur, and zero otherwise. Logging should go to standard error with timestamps and severity levels. ---

fetchimages.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line web image crawler. It should accept a starting URL and optional settings such as a maximum crawl depth, a maximum number of pages to visit, a restriction to the same domain, and a destination directory for downloaded files. Starting from the given page, the tool should fetch HTML pages, discover both hyperlinks to (including lazy-loading attributes, CSS-free image sources, and any base URL declared in the document), resolve relative addresses into absolute ones, and breadth-first traverse the site while avoiding revisiting the same page. For every discovered image, the script should download it, but only when the file extension or content indicates an image type from a common set of formats (such as JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, SVG, TIFF, ICO, and AVIF). Downloaded files should be saved into the output directory with safe, sanitized file names derived from the source URL, and duplicate images should be detected and skipped, for example by comparing content hashes. The tool should use a realistic browser-like user agent, handle network timeouts and HTTP errors gracefully without stopping the whole crawl, and respect a configurable delay between requests. The script should print progress information during the crawl and finish with a summary report listing the number of pages visited, images found, images saved, duplicates skipped, and errors encountered. Results should also be recorded in a manifest file mapping each saved image to its original URL and page of origin. Include clear help text for all command-line options and validate user inputs such as malformed URLs and invalid numeric limits before starting the crawl. ---

ffbp.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line file system utility for analyzing and cleaning up a project directory. The tool should accept a target directory (defaulting to the current working directory) and a set of options that control its behavior, parsed from the command line in a user-friendly way. Core capabilities it should provide: 1. **Human-readable size formatting**: Convert raw byte counts into compact, readable strings with appropriate units (bytes through terabytes, and beyond if needed), displayed with two decimal places. 2. **Extensionless Python script detection**: Identify files that have no file extension but are actually Python scripts. A file should qualify only if it is a regular file, is not inside a hidden directory or a cache directory, is not binary (no null bytes in its opening content), and begins with a shebang line referencing Python. Unreadable files should be safely skipped rather than crashing the tool. 3. **Backup file cleanup**: Recursively find all files ending in a `.bak` extension under the target directory, print each file's path relative to the target directory as it is removed, and delete it. 4. **Extension statistics**: Recursively scan the target directory and report, for a given file extension, the number of matching files and their total size, using the human-readable size format. The extension should be provided as a command-line argument and handled with or without a leading dot. Expected behavior: - Each capability should be selectable through a clear command-line option, with a helpful usage message and `--help` text. - Output should be concise, printed to standard output, with errors reported to standard error and a non-zero exit status on failure. - The tool should handle missing directories, permission errors, and invalid arguments gracefully without crashing. - Deletion of backup files should be performed carefully, reporting each removal so the user can see exactly what was changed. - The script should be runnable directly as a standalone program with a main entry point, and designed so the individual features can be reused or tested independently. ---

file_cleanup.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line utility for processing large text or data files efficiently. The tool should accept one or more input file paths and an output location as arguments, along with optional settings for character encoding, chunk size for batch processing, and the number of parallel workers. It should read input files robustly, including very large files, by choosing an efficient reading strategy based on file size so that memory usage stays bounded. The script should handle missing or unreadable files gracefully, reporting informational messages, warnings, and errors clearly to the user on the console, with errors going to the error stream. The core behavior is to process the input line by line or in chunks, optionally skipping empty lines, and to aggregate results such as line counts, word frequencies, or the most common tokens, using parallel processing where it helps throughput. Results should be written to the specified output in a structured, machine-readable format such as JSON, with a timestamp recording when the run occurred and a summary of the statistics gathered. The script should safely write output by using a temporary file and replacing the destination only upon successful completion, so partial results never corrupt an existing file. It should validate user-supplied arguments, provide helpful usage messages, and return meaningful exit codes indicating success, invalid input, or runtime failure. Design the solution so it is readable, modular, and easy to extend with additional analysis options, and include a clear command-line help description that explains each option. ---

filefixer.py: Write a Python script that acts as a file-type detection and classification tool for a directory tree or a set of files. Given one or more paths (files, directories, or archives), the tool should walk the contents, determine the true content type of each file, and report or organize results accordingly. Key requirements: - **Inputs:** Accept file and directory paths from the command line, with options to control recursion depth, include or exclude patterns, whether to inspect inside archives (zip, tar, tgz), and a parallelism level for speeding up large scans. Support a verbose or logging mode and a dry-run mode. - **Detection strategy:** Identify each file's type using multiple signals a fallback order: file extension (with normalization ofar.gz), magic-ines for scripts, and content heuristics for text versus binary. Use whichever optional detection backends are available in the environment, and degrade gracefully when they are not installed. Detect mismatches where the extension disagrees with the detected content and flag them. - **Text analysis:** For text-based source files such as Python, tokenize or otherwise parse the content safely to identify language and basic structure, handling encoding errors without crashing. - **Outputs:** Produce a structured report (human-readable table or summary plus a machine-readable format such as JSON) listing each file's path, declared extension, detected MIME type or language, binary/text classification, size, and any anomalies or mismatches. Optionally, support copying or moving files into folders grouped by detected type, respecting dry-run. - **Behavior:** Handle permissions errors, broken symlinks, and unreadable archives gracefully, logging problems and continuing. Never modify source files unless an explicit organize action is requested. Exit with a meaningful status code reflecting whether any errors or mismatches were found. - **Constraints:** Keep the tool self-contained and cross-platform, with clear help text describing every option and a concise summary printed at the end of each run. ---

filetools.py: Write a Python script that analyzes a directory tree on the local filesystem and reports on files whose creation (birth) time falls within a recent window, with optional handling of matching files based on that analysis. The tool should be a command-line utility that accepts a root directory path to scan, along with options controlling the time window (for example, a number of minutes or a fixed 24-hour lookback) and whether to only report or to take an action such as copying or moving the matching files to a destination folder. Key behaviors to include: - Recursively walk the given root directory, skipping version-control and Python cache directories so they never appear in results or get traversed. - For each file, determine its creation/birth timestamp where the operating system supports it (for example, on Linux via low-level file status queries), and fall back gracefully to another reasonable timestamp or skip the file when birth time is unavailable. Handle permission errors, broken symlinks, and files that disappear mid-scan without crashing. - Compare each file's creation time against the current UTC time and the requested window, selecting only the files created within it. - Process file checks in parallel using a bounded pool of workers to keep scanning fast on large trees, while showing a progress indicator in the terminal. - Display the results in a readable, color-coded terminal output that lists each matching file with its relative path and a human-readable creation timestamp, plus a summary count at the end. - When an action option is selected, copy or move the matching files into a specified output directory, preserving their relative directory structure, creating folders as needed, and avoiding overwriting existing files by renaming or reporting conflicts. - Validate all arguments up front, print clear error messages for invalid paths or options, and return appropriate exit codes (zero on success, non-zero on failure or invalid input). - Support a dry-run mode that reports what would be copied or moved without modifying the filesystem. - Keep the script self-contained, runnable directly from the command line, and well-documented with a helpful usage/help message. ---

fimport.py: Write a Python script that analyzes the source code of other Python files to detect import statements that are not placed at the module's top level, and reports them. The tool should accept one or more file or directory paths as input. When given a directory, it should recursively find all Python source files within it. For each file, it should parse the source into a syntax tree without executing it, then walk the tree to identify every import statement (both regular and "from ... import" forms) that appears nested inside a function, async function, class body, or control-flow block such as a loop, conditional, try/except, or with statement. Imports that sit directly at module level should be ignored. For each non-top-level import found, the script should output the file path, the line number, the import statement's source text or a normalized representation of the imported module names, and the enclosing context (such as the function or class name where it occurs), if feasible. Results should be printed in a clear, human-readable report grouped by file, with a summary count of total files scanned and total nested imports found. The script should handle errors gracefully: files that cannot be read or contain syntax errors should be reported as warnings without stopping the scan of other files. It should exit with a non-zero status code when nested imports are found, so it can be used in continuous integration pipelines, and zero when none are found. Provide an optional flag to output results as JSON for machine consumption. The script should be runnable from the command line, include a help message describing its usage, and be designed to be fast enough to scan large codebases. ---

furl_cli.py: Write a Python library that provides a simple, chainable interface for parsing, constructing, and manipulating URLs. The tool should accept a URL string (or individual URL components) and expose a mutable object whose parts can be read and modified: scheme, username, password, host, port, path segments, query parameters, and fragment. It should support adding, setting, removing, and reading query parameters, including repeated keys and ordered multi-value parameters, and it should allow path segments to be appended, replaced, or normalized (resolving "." and ".." segments). The object should be able to render itself back into a correctly encoded URL string, and should provide sensible default port handling for common schemes so that default ports can be omitted from the output. Include support for joining a relative URL onto a base URL, comparing URLs for equality, and producing deep copies so that modifications do not affect the original. Percent-encoding and decoding of path, query, and fragment components should be handled correctly, with control over which characters are treated as safe. Provide a clear, readable string representation and make the object work naturally with common Python idioms such as equality checks and copying. Handle malformed or incomplete input gracefully, emitting informative warnings where appropriate rather than crashing, and allow optional integration with a debugging helper if it is available, falling back to a no-op otherwise. The result should be a well-documented, dependency-light module that can be imported into other projects and used to build, inspect, and transform URLs in a fluent, object-oriented way. ---

furls.py: Write a Python script that scans a local directory tree (and optionally archive files within it) to discover and collect URLs and repository references from text-based content, then writes the findings into separate output files. The script should accept command-line arguments specifying the root directory to scan, an optional maximum file size limit in megabytes (with a sensible default of 15 MB), and options controlling how archives are handled. It should skip common version-control and cache directories such as those used by git and Python bytecode caches. Key behaviors: - Recursively walk the target directory, ignoring excluded directories, and read only files that are small enough to fit under the size limit. - Extract and search the contents of supported archive formats (including compressed tarballs, zip files, wheels, and other common compressed formats) using temporary working space that is cleaned up afterward, without leaving residue on disk. - Detect HTTP and HTTPS URLs in text, normalize them by stripping trailing punctuation and closing brackets, and de-duplicate results. - Identify git-style repository links (for example, entries referencing git submodules or repository remotes) and separate them from ordinary URLs. - Validate discovered URLs before recording them, using a helper for validity checking, and skip any that are malformed. - Append newly found URLs and repository references to two designated output text files, avoiding duplicates already present in those files from earlier runs. - Handle encoding errors, unreadable files, corrupt archives, and permission problems gracefully by logging a short warning and continuing the scan. - Print a concise summary at the end reporting how many files were scanned, how many archives were processed, and how many new URLs and repository links were added. - Keep all output messages and console feedback clear and minimal, suitable for use in automated pipelines. ---

fuzzy_dedup.py: Write a Python script that scans a directory tree and identifies duplicate and near-duplicate files, producing a clear report of the matches and optionally acting on them. The tool should accept a root directory path as its main input, along with options to control the scan, such as ignoring certain directory names (with sensible defaults for version control and dependency folders), following or skipping hidden files, setting a minimum file size, and choosing whether to include near-duplicates based on fuzzy similarity hashing in addition to exact duplicates identified by a fast non-cryptographic content hash. The user should be able to specify the similarity threshold for near-duplicate detection. The script should first group files by size to avoid unnecessary hashing, then compute content hashes for candidate files, and finally compare fuzzy hashes where requested. It should handle large directory trees efficiently, stream file contents rather than loading whole files into memory, and gracefully skip unreadable files or permission errors while reporting them. Outputs should include a human-readable summary printed to the console, with groups of duplicate files listed together along with their sizes and similarity scores where applicable. The tool should also support exporting results to a machine-readable format such as JSON or CSV, selected via a command-line option. An optional mode should allow moving or deleting redundant copies while always keeping one designated original per group, with a dry-run option that previews actions without modifying anything. Progress feedback should be shown during long scans when a terminal is attached, and the script should degrade gracefully if optional display libraries are unavailable. Required dependencies that are missing should produce a clear installation message and exit cleanly. ---

fuzzycmp.py: Write a Python script that acts as a text similarity and file comparison toolkit. It should let a user measure how alike two strings or two text files are, using a suite of well-known similarity and distance algorithms, and report the results clearly. Core purpose and capabilities: - Provide a collection of pluggable similarity and distance metrics for comparing texts. Cover edit-based measures (such as Levenshtein-style distances, including a transposition-aware variant and a longest-common-subsequence measure), token and set-based measures (such as Jaccard, Dice, cosine over token counts, and n-gram overlap), character-level measures suited to short names (such as Jaro and Jaro-Winkler), fuzzy matching measures that handle word reordering and partial substrings, Hamming distance for equal-length strings, and locality-sensitive hashing approaches for estimating similarity of large documents (such as MinHash and SimHash). - Include phonetic comparison options that encode words by how they sound (such as Soundex, Metaphone, and NYSIIS) so that spelling variants of the same name can be matched. - Offer a common interface so that every metric can be applied uniformly, and allow a user to choose one or several metrics at run time. - Support text normalization before comparison, including optional case folding, whitespace collapsing, punctuation removal, and a default word-level tokenizer. Inputs: - Command-line usage that accepts either two literal strings or two file paths, a choice of metric (or all default metrics), and options such as normalization toggles, n-gram size, and other metric parameters. - File comparison should read two text files, optionally align them line by line, and produce per-line or whole-file results. Outputs: - Human-readable console output showing each metric's score for the comparison, with clear labeling of whether a higher value means more similar or more different. - For file comparison, a summary of similarity plus a line-level diff report that marks inserted, deleted, replaced, and unchanged lines. - Sensible handling of errors such as missing files, unreadable input, or unknown metric names, with informative messages and a non-zero exit status. Key behaviors: - Metrics must return consistent, documented ranges where possible, and handle edge cases such as empty strings, identical inputs, and very long texts without crashing. - Randomized estimators (such as MinHash) should accept a seed so results are reproducible. - Provide a help screen describing all options and available metrics. - The script should be self-contained, runnable directly from the command line, and organized so that new metrics can be added easily. ---

fv.py: Write a Python script that takes a single file path from the command line, reads the file's text content (tolerating invalid or non-UTF-8 bytes without crashing), and displays the content in an interactive, scrollable pager so the user can page through long documents comfortably. The script should be runnable directly from a terminal, exit cleanly when the viewer is closed, and handle the case where the required file argument is missing by showing a brief usage message. Keep the tool minimal and dependency-free, with the focus on quick, read-only viewing of text files. ---

fztrans.py: Write a Python script that acts as an interactive command-line bilingual dictionary lookup tool between Persian (Farsi) and English. The tool should load its word data from a JSON dictionary file stored in the user's home directory, where each entry maps a Persian word to its English equivalent. If the dictionary file is missing or cannot be parsed, the tool should report a clear error message to the user and exit gracefully. Key behaviors to include: - Support both directions of lookup: the user can enter a Persian word and receive its English translation, or enter an English word and receive its Persian equivalent. The tool should automatically detect which language the input belongs to. - Provide an interactive prompt loop that keeps running until the user chooses to quit, with simple exit commands. - Offer tab-completion or autocomplete for known words in both languages to make lookups faster and reduce typing errors. - When a word is not found exactly, suggest close matches (fuzzy matching) from the dictionary so the user can correct a typo. - Allow the tool to be invoked directly with a word as a command-line argument for a one-off lookup, in addition to the interactive mode. - Include an option to display the translation using an external formatting or display helper when available, falling back gracefully when it is not installed. - Handle keyboard interruptions and end-of-input signals cleanly without crashing. - Log informational and error messages through a consistent logging setup rather than unstructured printing where appropriate. - Handle Persian text correctly with UTF-8 encoding throughout. The output for each lookup should clearly show the query, the matched translation, and any suggestions when no exact match exists. Keep the design modular and readable, with the core lookup logic separated from the user interface layer. ---

g1.py: Write a Python script that acts as a GitHub repository cloning and mirroring utility. It should accept a GitHub repository reference (SSH URL, HTTPS URL, or owner/name shorthand) along with a target directory and optional settings such as branch, clone depth, and which backend tool to use for cloning. The script should clone the repository into the target location, shallowly by default, and resolve the default branch automatically via the GitHub API when no branch is specified, falling back to a sensible default if resolution fails. The script should support multiple interchangeable cloning backends, selectable by name, with a sensible default. It should be designed around a common interface so that each backend can be swapped without changing the rest of the workflow. Where a backend does not support a given operation, the script should degrade gracefully or report a clear error. Handle submodules: if the repository contains a submodules configuration file, the script should detect the submodules and initialize, update, and recursively fetch them as needed, with the option to skip this step. Include a size-aware behavior: estimate or check the repository size via the GitHub API, and when it exceeds a configurable threshold (default 5 MB), switch to a lighter-weight strategy such as a shallower or partial clone, and log that decision. Provide clear logging of each step (resolution, cloning, submodule handling, errors), using a structured logging approach. Validate inputs up front, normalize URLs, and fail with informative messages when the repository is inaccessible, the target already exists in an incompatible state, or required external tools are missing. Use an optional GitHub access token from the environment for authenticated API calls and private repositories, and never print the token. Expose all behavior through a command-line interface with help text, sensible defaults, and exit codes that indicate success or the category of failure. Optionally support a dry-run mode that reports what would be done without modifying the filesystem. Keep the code modular, well-documented, and suitable for use both as a standalone CLI and as an importable module. ---

gdetect_dup_objects.py: Write a Python script that analyzes Python source files to detect whether they use type annotations, and reports or optionally removes those annotations to produce an unannotated version of the code. The tool should accept one or more Python file paths (or a directory to scan recursively) as input and process each file independently. Key behaviors: - Parse each Python source file into a syntactic representation without executing it, and walk the structure to determine whether any function signatures (parameters, keyword-only parameters, variadic arguments, return types) or variable declarations carry type annotations. - Produce a per-file result indicating whether annotations were found, and summarize results across all processed files in a machine-readable format (such as JSON) written to standard output or a specified output file. - Provide an optional mode that strips all type annotations from function signatures and variable declarations while preserving the original logic, formatting where possible, and valid Python syntax, then writes the cleaned code to a new file or overwrites the original only when explicitly requested. - Handle both synchronous and asynchronous function definitions consistently. - Process files in parallel using multiple worker processes when many files are provided, while keeping results deterministic and ordered by input path. - Gracefully report files that fail to parse (e.g., syntax errors, encoding problems) without aborting the overall run, and include the error details in the output. - Return a non-zero exit status if any file could not be processed, and zero otherwise. - Include a command-line interface with clear help text, options for output location, recursive directory scanning, dry-run behavior, and worker count configuration. ---

gdrive_sync.py: Write a Python script that backs up files from a user's Google Drive to a local directory. The tool should authenticate the user with Google OAuth using a read-only Drive scope, remember the authorization between runs so the user does not have to log in every time, and load optional settings such as credential file locations, token storage, and backup destination from a configuration file or environment variables, falling back to sensible defaults when they are absent. The script should accept command-line options that let the user choose which Drive content to back up, such as a specific folder, the entire "My Drive," or files matching certain criteria, and should allow the user to specify the local output directory. It should walk through Drive folders recursively, recreate the folder hierarchy locally, and download regular files. Google-native documents (such as Docs, Sheets, and Slides) should be exported to standard formats like PDF, DOCX, XLSX, or PPTX, while binary files should be downloaded as-is. Large files should be downloaded in chunks with progress reporting. The tool should handle pagination of Drive listings, skip files that are already up to date by comparing modification timestamps with previously downloaded copies, and resume or safely retry after transient network or API errors. It should record a summary of what was downloaded, skipped, and failed, and report clear, human-readable error messages for authentication failures, permission issues, missing files, and quota limits. It should support a dry-run mode that lists what would be backed up without writing any files, and a verbose mode that shows detailed progress. The script should be runnable from the command line, exit with meaningful status codes on success or failure, and include helpful usage documentation so a user can understand every option without reading the source. ---

gdupfunc.py: Write a Python script that scans a project directory tree for Python source files and reports how consistently they use type annotations. The tool should accept a root directory path as its main input, along with optional settings for additional directory names to skip and a minimum size threshold so that trivially small files are ignored. By default it should skip common non-source folders such as version control metadata, virtual environments, caches, build artifacts, and dependency directories. For each qualifying Python file, the script should parse the source safely, determine whether the file contains any type annotations on function parameters, return values, or variadic arguments (for both regular and async functions), and classify the file as annotated or unannotated. Files that cannot be parsed due to syntax errors should be recorded as skipped with a reason rather than causing the whole run to fail. Files that are too small to be meaningful should also be excluded from the statistics. The script should process files efficiently, potentially in parallel for large projects, and produce a summary report containing the total number of files analyzed, how many are annotated versus unannotated, the overall annotation coverage percentage, and a list of the unannotated files with their relative paths. It should support a machine-readable JSON output option in addition to a human-readable console output, and it should write its results to stdout or to a specified output file. The command-line interface should provide clear help text, validate that the provided path exists and is a directory, and return a non-zero exit code on invalid input or unrecoverable errors. Include a quiet mode that suppresses progress messages and a verbose mode that lists every analyzed file with its status. ---

gdupfx.py: Write a Python script that scans one or more directory trees on the local filesystem and identifies duplicate files, reporting them so the user can review or clean up wasted disk space. The tool should be a command-line utility that accepts one or more root directories to scan, along with options to control recursion depth, skip common version-control, dependency, and cache folders by default (with the ability to include or exclude additional paths or patterns), set a minimum file size threshold, and optionally follow or ignore symbolic links.
