The script should work efficiently on large directory trees by first grouping files by size, since files of different sizes cannot be identical, and only then comparing candidates more deeply. For candidates sharing a size, it should use a quick partial comparison (for example, hashing a small sample of each file) to eliminate most non-duplicates before performing a full content comparison using a fast, non-cryptographic hashing algorithm or a byte-by-byte check, reading files in chunks so that memory usage stays low regardless of file size. The work should be parallelized across multiple threads to speed up I/O-bound hashing, with a sensible default worker count that the user can override. The output should present each set of duplicate files together, showing the file size, the number of copies, the total reclaimable space, and the full paths of every copy, ordered so that the largest wasted-space groups appear first. The tool should also provide a summary at the end with the total number of files scanned, the number of duplicate groups found, the total reclaimable space, and the elapsed time. Support a machine-readable output format (such as JSON) in addition to human-readable text, and optionally write results to a file. Include a safe, non-destructive default mode, and an optional mode that interactively or via flag removes duplicates while always keeping one designated copy per group (for example, the first or oldest one), with a dry-run option that shows what would be deleted without changing anything. Handle permission errors, unreadable files, broken symbolic links, and files that change during the scan gracefully by logging a warning and continuing rather than aborting. Provide clear error messages for invalid arguments or missing directories, and exit with appropriate status codes. Ensure the script is robust, cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux), and reports progress to the user during long scans without cluttering machine-readable output. ---

get_latest_pkgs_added_to_pypi.py: Write a Python script that fetches the latest package release updates from the PyPI (Python Package Index) RSS feed, parses the feed, and exports the results to a structured file for later analysis. The script should: - Retrieve the current package updates feed from the official PyPI website over the network, handling connection problems, timeouts, and bad HTTP responses gracefully with clear error messages. - Parse the feed's XML content and extract, for each entry, the key details: package or release title, link, description, publication date, and a unique identifier. - Skip entries that lack a meaningful title, and normalize missing fields to empty values so the output stays consistent. - Present the collected records in a clean, human-readable form and also save them to a file in a machine-friendly format (such as CSV or JSON), using a sensible default filename that the user can override from the command line. - Convert publication timestamps into a readable, consistent date-time representation where possible, and fall back to the raw value if conversion is not possible. - Accept optional command-line arguments that allow the user to choose the output format, set the output file path, limit the number of results shown, and filter entries by a keyword matched against package names or descriptions. - Print a concise summary at the end indicating how many entries were found, how many were kept after filtering, and where the output was saved. - Exit with a non-zero status code and a helpful message if the feed cannot be retrieved or parsed, and exit cleanly on user interruption. Keep the solution self-contained, well-organized into reusable parts, and suitable for running from a terminal on any major operating system. ---

get_lic.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line license file generator. It should accept a license type chosen from a set of available license templates stored in a local "files" folder (the license type names are derived from the template file names), along with the holder's name and a year or date to be filled in. The tool should produce the completed license text, printing it to the terminal or saving it to an output file the user specifies. To make repeated use faster, the script should remember the most recently used license details in a small cache file stored in the user's home directory. On each run it should check whether the requested details match what is cached: on a hit, it reuses the cached values and reports that a cache hit occurred; on a miss, it asks for or accepts the needed details, generates the license, and updates the cache, reporting the miss. Cache hits and misses should be shown to the user with colored, easy-to-read status messages. Handle errors gracefully with a clearly formatted, colored error message. This includes an unknown or unsupported license type (the message should list the valid options), a missing or unreadable template, an invalid or malformed date or year, and a missing or unwritable cache file. Validate user input before generating output, and make sure a failure never leaves a corrupted cache or a partially written output file. The interface should be a clean command-line experience with helpful `--help` text, sensible defaults where reasonable, and clear success conf self-contained, cross-platform where practical, and organized so the template discovery, cache handling, input validation, and text generation are easy to follow and maintain. ---

get_pypi_rssfeed.py: Write a Python script that fetches the latest package updates from the PyPI RSS feed (https://pypi.org/rss/packages.xml), parses the feed, and presents the newly published or recently updated Python packages in a clear, readable form. The script should retrieve the feed over the network with a sensible timeout, handle connection and HTTP errors gracefully by reporting them to the error stream and exiting cleanly without crashing, and validate that the received content is a well-formed RSS document with a channel and items. For each package entry, extract its title (package name and version), link to the PyPI project page, description summary, and publication date, using sensible defaults such as "Unknown" or "No description" when fields are missing. Normalize the publication dates so they can be displayed consistently and sorted from most recent to oldest. Output the results to standard output as a formatted list or table that a user can scan quickly, optionally limiting the number of entries shown through a command-line argument, and optionally allowing the user to filter packages by a keyword matched against names or descriptions. Ensure the script runs as a standalone command-line tool, includes helpful usage information, and handles malformed or unexpected feed entries without interrupting the overall output. ---

get_sub.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for automatically downloading sub video files. The tool should accept one or more video file paths (or a directory to scan recursively) and, for each video, determine its identity (title, season, episode, release group, etc.) from the filename using intelligent filename parsing. It should then search one or more online subtitle providers for matching subtitles in the requested language(s), select the best match, and download it. Subtitles that arrive as compressed archives (zip, rar, or 7z) should be extracted automatically, and the subtitle file should be saved alongside the video using a naming convention that matches the video's base name and language code. Supported subtitle formats include common text and bitmap subtitle types, and supported video formats include a wide range of common container extensions. Key behaviors to cover: - Accept command-line options for target languages (multiple allowed), provider selection, a force-overwrite option, a dry-run or preview mode, verbosity or quiet logging, and a version flag. - Skip videos that already have a matching subtitle unless forced to overwrite. - Handle network failures, rate limits, and provider errors gracefully with retries and clear messages, continuing with remaining files rather than aborting the whole batch. - Provide a progress or summary report at the end listing successes, skips, and failures. - Optionally support a configuration file for default languages, providers, and credentials, and support for external tools required to extract RAR archives where applicable. - Use a web-scraping or API approach to query subtitle sites, parse their HTML or JSON responses, and handle site-specific differences through a pluggable provider design. - Produce a clean, user-friendly console output, and exit with a meaningful status code reflecting overall success or failure. ---

get_trending_py_repos.py: Write a Python script that scrapes the trending Python repositories page on GitHub for three time windows (daily, weekly, and monthly) and saves the results to structured files. The script should request each trending page with a sensible timeout and handle HTTP errors gracefully, then parse the returned HTML to extract, for each repository, its owner/name, full URL, description, primary programming language, and any other visible metadata such as star count, fork count, and stars gained during the period. Entries with missing optional fields should still be recorded with empty or default values rather than causing failures. The script should organize its output in a dedicated output directory, creating it if it does not exist, and produce one file per timeframe in a machine-friendly format such as CSV and JSON, with consistent column names and a clear, predictable structure. It should print a concise progress summary to the console indicating how many repositories were found for each timeframe and where the files were saved. Design the script so that the set of timeframes and the output location are easy to change, and include a clear top-level entry point that runs the full collection process when the script is executed directly. Prioritize robustness against network failures and changes in page layout, and keep the code readable and well-documented with brief comments explaining each major step. ---

getpyrepos.py: Write a Python script that fetches all public repositories for a given GitHub username, keeps only those whose primary language is Python, and outputs a structured summary of each matching repository. The script should accept the GitHub username as a command-line argument, handle pagination automatically so that users with many repositories are fully covered, and sort or present results by most recently updated. For each repository, capture its name, full name, description (with a sensible fallback when missing), web URL, star count, fork count, primary language, creation and last-update timestamps, and visibility status. Output the collected results as well-formatted JSON to standard output, and optionally allow the user to save them to a file. Handle errors gracefully, including network failures, HTTP errors such as unknown users or rate limiting, and invalid responses, reporting clear messages to the user and exiting with a non-zero status code when something goes wrong. If no Python repositories are found, the script should still produce a valid, empty result rather than crashing. Include a brief usage message when the username argument is missing or invalid. ---

getrepos.py: Write a Python script that connects to the GitHub API to retrieve the list of repositories belonging to a specified user account. The script should accept a GitHub username as input, along with an optional access token loaded from environment configuration or supplied directly, so that authenticated requests can be made for higher rate limits and access to private repositories the token permits. It should allow a configurable network timeout for API requests. While the request is in progress, the script should display a live countdown in the terminal that updates each second and then clears itself once the operation completes, running in a way that does not block the main work. If the user has no repositories, the script should print a clear message stating that no repositories were found for that username and return an empty result. When repositories are found, the script should gather their key details, such as names, descriptions, visibility, primary language, star and fork counts, and last-updated timestamps, and return them in a structured form that can be displayed on screen or exported to a file in a common machine-readable format. The script should handle common failure cases gracefully, including invalid or nonexistent usernames, expired or invalid tokens, network interruptions, and API rate-limit errors, presenting a helpful error message to the user instead of crashing with an unhandled traceback. It should be runnable from the command line, accepting the username and optional flags for token and timeout, and should ensure that sensitive credentials are never printed to the console or written to output files. ---

getsub.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line subtitle downloader for video files. It should accept a media title (or a path to a video file from which a title can be derived), an optional season and episode number, and a preferred subtitle language and file extension. The tool should normalize the title by replacing separators such as underscores and dots with spaces, then search a configurable set of online subtitle providers (defaulting to OpenSubtitles, Podnapisi, Addic7ed, and TVSubtitles) for matching subtitle files. It should support two modes: a file mode that takes a local video file, infers its metadata, and downloads a matching subtitle saved alongside the video, and a search mode that queries by title alone and saves the best result under a sanitized, filesystem-safe filename derived from the title, ensuring the correct file extension is appended. The script should validate user inputs such as the extension (rejecting empty values and normalizing a leading dot), handle missing optional dependencies gracefully with clear error messages, use a realistic browser user-agent when making web requests, log progress and failures using standard logging levels, respect a verbose flag for debug output, and return meaningful exit codes. It should fail gracefully on network errors, unmatched results, or unsupported providers, and report to the user which subtitle file was saved and where. ---

gexcst.py: Write a Python script that analyzes a collection of Python source archives and packages, extracts the top-level and nested definitions (classes, functions, and similar named code entities) from every Python source file found inside them, and saves each extracted entity as its own individual file in an organized output directory. The script should accept one or more input paths pointing to archive files (such as wheels, zip files, and various tarball formats including compressed variants) or to directories containing such archives or loose Python files. It should unpack or read each archive safely, skipping non-Python content, and process only files with Python source extensions or extensionless files that are plausibly Python code. For each Python file, the script should parse the source using a concrete syntax tree approach that preserves original formatting, and track each entity's exact position in the source so that its original text can be reproduced faithfully, including its indentation and surrounding structure. Each extracted entity should be recorded with metadata describing its name, kind, nesting depth, and the file it originated from. The script should write each extracted entity to a file in the output directory, using a clear and filesystem-safe naming scheme that avoids collisions, such as incorporating the originating package or archive name, the source module path, and the entity name. It should also produce a summary index or manifest describing all extracted entities and their locations. Use multiprocessing to parallelize processing across archives or files to take advantage of available CPU cores, with a sensible default worker count that can be configured. The script should be robust: a malformed or unparseable file or a corrupted archive must be logged and skipped without halting the entire run. It should report progress and a final summary of how many archives, files, and entities were processed and how many failures occurred. Provide a command-line interface that accepts the input paths, an optional output directory, an optional worker count, and an option to control whether nested entities (such as methods inside classes) are extracted in addition to top-level ones. Clean up any temporary extraction directories when processing finishes, even if errors occur. ---

gext.py: Write a Python script that scans one or more user-supplied file or directory paths for Python source files, analyzes each file's structure, and extracts its classes, top-level functions, and constants into separate organized output files. The tool should: - Accept a list of input paths (command-line arguments) that may be individual files or directories. When a directory is given, search it recursively for Python sources, skipping common non-source folders such as test, example, and output directories. - Identify Python files either by their `.py` extension or by a Python shebang line on the first line, so that extensionless executable scripts are also included. - Parse each discovered file safely, tolerating files that have syntax errors or unreadable encodings by reporting and skipping them without stopping the whole run. - Extract three categories of definitions: class definitions (with their source code), function definitions (with their source code), and module-level constant assignments (with their source code), recording the originating file for each item. - Write each category to its own dedicated output directory under a common `output` folder, producing one file per extracted item in a readable, consistently named format that avoids filename collisions across source files. - Process files in parallel using a pool of multiple worker processes to speed up work on large codebases, and ensure the output is safe on all platforms. - Print a concise progress and summary report at the end, including the number of files scanned, items extracted per category, and any files that failed to process. - Handle edge cases gracefully: empty inputs, nonexistent paths, and duplicate names across files should not crash the program. ---

gext0.py: Write a Python script that analyzes a collection of Python source packages and archives and extracts the individual code entities (such as classes, functions, and their source definitions) from them, saving each extracted entity as its own organized output file. The tool should accept a directory of inputs that may contain raw Python source files as well as compressed or packaged archives (such as zip files, wheels, and various tarball formats including gzip, xz, and zstd compressed tars). It should recursively discover these inputs, unpack archives into a temporary working area, and then process only Python source files and extensionless files that appear to be Python code, ignoring other file types. For each Python source file, the script should parse the code into its syntactic structure and identify top-level and nested definitions, including classes, functions, and methods, while tracking the scope depth of each one. For every identified entity, it should capture the exact original source text of that definition, along with metadata such as the entity's name, type, starting and ending line numbers, the originating file path, and its parent scope. Files that cannot be parsed as valid Python should be skipped gracefully with a logged warning rather than halting the whole run. The results should be written to an output directory, organized so that entities are grouped by their originating package or archive and remain easy to browse. Each extracted entity should be saved in a clearly named file, and a summary index or manifest should be produced listing all extracted entities with their metadata and counts of processed files, skipped files, and errors. Because the input set may be large, the script should take advantage of parallel processing across available CPU cores to speed up extraction, while keeping results deterministic and safely aggregated. It must clean up temporary extraction directories when finished, even if errors occur, and should protect against unsafe archive members such as path traversal attempts or absolute paths within archives. Provide clear command-line options for specifying the input location, the output location, and optionally the number of worker processes, and include informative progress and error reporting throughout the run. ---

gfco.py: Write a Python script that converts font files between common web and desktop font formats. The tool should accept one or more font files (or a directory containing font files) as input, along with a target format chosen from TTF, OTF, WOFF, WOFF2, and EOT. For each input file, it should produce a converted copy in the requested format, preserving the font's glyphs, metrics, and naming data as faithfully as possible. The user should be able to specify an optional output directory; if none is given, the converted file should be saved alongside the original. The tool should validate that the target format is supported and that each source file exists and is a recognized font type, skipping or reporting unsupported files without stopping the entire batch. It should also offer an option to delete the original source file after a successful conversion, and should only do so when the conversion has completed successfully. For large batches, the script should process files concurrently to reduce total runtime, using a reasonable degree of parallelism that is safe for CPU-bound font processing. It should report progress and a clear summary at the end, listing which files converted successfully, which were skipped, and which failed along with a brief reason for each. If a required dependency for font processing is missing, the script should exit with a clear, human-readable message explaining how to install it. The command-line interface should be simple and self-documenting, with help text describing each argument, and it should return a non-zero exit status if any conversion fails. ---

ghpy.py: Write a Python script that queries the GitHub repository search API to retrieve the 50 most recently updated public repositories written in Python, then saves a human-readable summary report of those results to a local text file and confirms the save location to the user. The script should: - Load credentials from a environment configuration file located in the user's home directory, reading a GitHub access token from it so the API request is authenticated. - Request up to 50 Python repositories, sorted by most recent update time in descending order. - Handle HTTP errors from the API by surfacing a clear failure rather than silently producing an incomplete file. - Write the output to a plain text file named "ghpy.txt" in the current working directory. The file should begin with a title line indicating it contains the 50 most active Python repositories, followed by a visual separator. - For each repository, record its full name (owner/repo), its web URL, its last updated timestamp, and its star count each onented line, with a blank line between entries. - Print a confirmation message to the console indicating where the results were saved. - Include a standard main-entry guard so the search runs only when the file is executed directly. ---

ghpy10.py: Write a Python script that searches GitHub for the most popular recently created Python repositories and saves a summary list to a local text file. The script should load a GitHub access token from a user-level environment configuration file in the home directory, and fail with a clear error message if the token is missing. It should query GitHub's repository search service for Python-language projects created within roughly the last ten days, ranked by star count in descending order, retrieving up to fifty results per request. Each matching repository's full name (owner and repository name) should be written, one per line, to an output file named "ghpy10.txt" in the current working directory. The script should handle failed API responses by surfacing the error rather than silently writing incomplete output, and should be runnable as a standalone command-line tool with no required arguments. ---

ghzip.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for preparing and fetching GitHub repository content. The tool should accept a repository reference in either short form (owner/name) or as a full GitHub URL, normalize it into a canonical form, and validate that it is well-formed, rejecting malformed input with a clear error message. The script should optionally read a GitHub access token from the environment or from a local `.env` file in the user's home directory, and use it to authenticate requests so that private repositories and higher API rate limits are supported. If no token is available, it should still work for public repositories. Its main purpose is to retrieve the contents of a target repository (or a specified branch, tag, or subdirectory) and save them to a local output location chosen by the user via command-line arguments. It should support selecting a fetch backend, with a sensible default that uses a system command-line git client, and allow the user to switch to an alternative backend that talks to the GitHub API directly. The tool should handle large files gracefully, for example by skipping or warning about files above a size threshold of roughly 5 MB unless the user explicitly opts in. Key behaviors: - Parse and validate command-line arguments, including the repository, optional ref, destination path, backend choice, token override, and any filtering or size-limit options, with helpful `--help` output. - Show progress or status messages to the user while working, and report a concise summary at the end (files written, files skipped, total size). - Fail with non-zero exit codes and readable error messages for invalid input, network or authentication failures, missing tools, and existing non-empty destinations (unless an overwrite option is given). - Avoid leaking the access token in logs or error output. - Be safe with file paths: prevent writing outside the chosen destination directory, even if repository contents contain unusual paths. - Keep the implementation self-contained, cross-platform (Linux, macOS, Windows), and easy to run with a standard Python 3 interpreter, with optional dependencies handled gracefully when missing. ---

gitclone.py: Write a Python script that acts as a convenient git clone helper. It takes a repository URL and an optional target directory name from the command line, automatically detects the remote repository's default branch, and clones it with a single shallow-style, branch-specific operation. If no URL is provided, it should display a brief usage message and exit with an error status. If the default branch cannot be determined (for example, the URL is unreachable or invalid), it should print a clear error message to the standard error stream and exit with a failure status. When no target directory is given, the script should derive a sensible local folder name from the last path segment of the URL, stripping any trailing slashes and a trailing ".git" suffix. After a successful clone, the script should check whether the repository contains submodules and, if so, initialize and update them recursively. It should report progress and the final location of the cloned repository to the user in a concise, friendly way, and return an appropriate exit code indicating success or failure of each step. Errors from the underlying git operations should be surfaced to the user rather than silently ignored. ---

gitrepos.py: Write a Python script that fetches the public repositories of a given GitHub user and saves a readable summary of them to a text file. The tool should accept a GitHub username and an optional output file path, retrieving the user's repository list from GitHub's public API and handling network or API errors gracefully with informative messages. If the user has no public repositories, the tool should report that clearly and exit without creating a misleading output file. For each repository, the summary should include key details such as its name, description (with a sensible fallback when none is provided), web URL, star count, fork count, and primary programming language (with a fallback when unspecified). The output file should begin with a header identifying the GitHub user and be written using UTF-8 encoding so that non-ASCII descriptions are preserved. The script should be robust to missing or null fields in the API response, produce a clean and easy-to-scan layout, and be usable both as a standalone command-line utility and as a reusable function that other code can call. ---

gittools.py: Write a Python script that acts as a batch Git repository maintenance and reporting tool. It should accept a root directory (or a list of repository paths) as input, automatically discover Git repositories within it, and for each repository determine its current branch (handling detached HEAD states gracefully), check the working tree status, and gather basic synchronization information with the configured remote. The tool should run these operations concurrently across repositories to keep execution fast, enforce sensible timeouts so a hung Git command never blocks the whole run, and isolate failures so that one broken repository does not stop the others from being processed. The script should be runnable from the command line with options such as a target path, a flag to limit or skip certain directories, a maximum number of parallel workers, and an output format choice (human-readable text or machine-readable JSON). It should aggregate the results into a clear summary report that lists each repository with its branch, cleanliness state, count of uncommitted or untracked changes, and whether it is ahead of or behind its upstream, and it should highlight repositories that need attention. Exit codes should reflect whether any repository had errors or required action. Handle edge cases robustly: missing Git installation, non-repository directories, nested repositories, repositories without a remote or upstream, permission errors, and unexpected command output. Provide informative error messages without exposing raw stack traces to the user unless a verbose mode is requested. Optionally, the tool may support a dry-run mode that reports what would be fetched or updated without modifying anything, and it should never make destructive changes to repositories by default. Include clear help text documenting every option, and keep the code modular, readable, and well-documented so it can be extended with additional Git checks later. ---

gll.py: Write a Python script that extracts a range of lines from a text file given on the command line and saves that excerpt to a new output file. The tool should accept a file path, a starting line number, and an optional ending line number. If the end line is omitted, the excerpt should run from the start line through the end of the file. Requirements: - **Inputs:** A source filename, a 1-based start line, and an optional inclusive end line, all supplied as command-line arguments. Print a short usage message to standard error and exit with a non-zero status if the required arguments are missing. - **Validation:** Reject non-integer line numbers, a start line below 1, and an end line smaller than the start line. Report each problem with a clear error message on standard error and exit with a non-zero status. Also report an error if the source file does not exist or is not a regular file. - **Output:** Write the selected lines to a new file in the current working directory that keeps the original file's extension. Name the output by the line range, using the form `<start><ext>` when no end line is given and `<start>_<end><ext>` when one is given. - **Text handling:** Read the source as UTF-8 text, tolerating invalid byte sequences without crashing, and write the output as UTF-8. - **Behavior:** Copy lines exactly as they appear, preserving their original line endings and content. Handle files shorter than the requested range gracefully by copying whatever lines exist. Exit with status 0 on success. - **Robustness:** Handle file read and write errors gracefully with informative messages rather than unhandled exceptions. - **Style:** Keep the script self-contained, runnable as a standalone command-line program, and clearly documented with a brief usage description. ---

gp.py: Write a Python script that automatically stages and commits all changes in the Git repository the user is currently working in. The tool should locate the enclosing repository even if the user runs it from a subdirectory, and it should fail gracefully with a clear message on stderr and a non-zero exit status if the current location is not inside a valid Git repository or the repository cannot be accessed. Before committing, the script should check whether a `.gitignore` file exists in the current working directory. If none exists, it should attempt to seed the project with the user's global `.gitignore` from the home directory, silently skipping this step if the global file is missing or unreadable, and never overwriting an existing local `.gitignore`. Once the repository is ready, the script should stage all tracked and untracked changes (including deletions) and create a single commit whose message is "Auto-commit" followed by the current local date and time in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. Its behavior should be non-interactive, suitable for running from scripts, cron jobs, or a shell alias. Any errors during staging or committing should be reported to stderr with a descriptive message and a non-zero exit status, without leaving the repository in a partially modified state where feasible. The output should be minimal: on success, the script should print nothing to stdout or only a brief confirmation, while all diagnostic and error information goes to stderr. The script should be a single, self-contained file that runs with a standard Python 3 interpreter and relies only on widely available third-party Git tooling for repository operations. ---

grmc.py: Python Comment & Docstring Stripper (Tree-sitter & LibCST based)

grmcst.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line tool for stripping comments and docstrings from Python source files while ke code's behavior intact. The tool should accept one or more file or directory paths as input, recursively discover Python files within directories, and process each file independently so that large batches run quickly by using parallel workers with a sensible upper limit on concurrency. For each file, the script should parse the source in a way that preserves its structure and formatting as much as possible, then remove ordinary comments while retaining special directive comments that tools and interpreters depend on: shebang lines, type annotations comments, and formatter control markers such as those that turn formatting on or off or skip a single statement. Module, class, and function docstrings (the leading string literals in those bodies) should also be removed, leaving the remaining code valid and runnable. The script should be careful not to break syntax when a block would otherwise become empty, for example by substituting a harmless placeholder statement where needed. The tool should support an option to write changes back in place, an option to print a unified diff or summary of what would change without modifying files (a dry-run mode), and an option to write output to a specified destination directory while preserving relative paths. It should report a clear summary at the end, including how many files were scanned, modified, skipped, and any files that failed to parse, and it should exit with a nonzero status code when errors occur. Malformed or non-UTF-8 files must be handled gracefully with a descriptive message rather than crashing the whole batch. Output should be deterministic so that running the tool twice on the same input produces identical results. ---

group_by_size.py: Write a Python script that organizes the subdirectories of the current working directory into a fixed number of balanced group folders based on their total size. The script should accept a single command-line argument specifying how many groups (parts) to create, with a sensible default and validation for invalid values. Behavior requirements: - Scan only the immediate subdirectories of the current working directory, ignoring regular files and any existing folders whose names begin with "group_" so that repeated runs do not reorganize previous output. - For each candidate subdirectory, compute its total size by recursively summing the sizes of all files it contains, tolerating permission errors or files that disappear mid-scan by skipping them rather than crashing. - Report to the user how many subdirectories were found and, for each one, its name and size in megabytes with two decimal places. If no qualifying subdirectories exist, print a clear message and exit gracefully. - Distribute the subdirectories across the requested number of groups so that the combined sizes of the groups are as close to equal as possible. A greedy strategy that assigns the largest remaining directory to the currently lightest group is an acceptable approach, but the outcome should be a balanced split. - Create each group as a new folder named with the "group_" prefix followed by its index, and move each assigned subdirectory into its group folder. Handle the case where the requested number of groups exceeds the number of subdirectories gracefully (for example, by creating only as many groups as needed or warning the user). - Print a summary after the operation showing each group's folder name, the directories it received, and its total size in megabytes. - Handle errors such as permission problems or name collisions during moves with informative messages, continuing with the remaining work where safely possible rather than aborting the entire run. - The script should be runnable directly from the command line and should not require any input beyond its arguments. ---

gsz.py: Write a Python script that takes a GitHub repository reference from the user and reports the repository's size. The user can supply the reference either as a full GitHub URL (such as a link to the repository's main page) or as a short "owner/repository" pair. The script should validate the input format and print a clear error message if the reference is malformed. It should then look up the repository's metadata through GitHub's public API, handle the case where the repository does not exist with a friendly "not found" message, and handle network or other API failures gracefully without crashing. When the lookup succeeds, the script should display the repository's full name in the form owner/repository and its size converted to megabytes, rounded to two decimal places. The script should be runnable from the command line with the repository reference provided as an argument, and it should keep its output concise and human-readable. ---

gtransline.py: Write a Python script that scans a project directory for source files containing Chinese text and automatically translates that text into English, producing a translated copy or in-place update while preserving the overall structure and meaning of the files. The tool should accept a target directory (or file path) and optional settings from the command line, such as whether to modify files in place, an output location, and a flag for a dry-run mode that only reports what would change. It should recursively walk the directory tree while skipping common non-source or cache folders (for example version control, build caches, linter caches, and similar generated directories). Key behaviors: - Detect whether a piece of text is predominantly Chinese, using a configurable ratio threshold so that mixed or mostly-English content is handled sensibly. - Identify translatable Chinese segments within files, such as comments, strings, and docstrings, and leave the surrounding code syntax intact so that files remain valid and runnable after translation. - Use an available third-party translation backend; if none of the supported translation libraries is installed, it should log a clear installation message and exit with a non-zero status. Support fallback between at least two translation backends. - Process multiple files concurrently to speed up large projects, with sensible worker-count defaults and a way to override it. - Handle encoding issues gracefully, preserve original line endings and file formatting where possible, and skip binary or unreadable files with a warning. - Log progress and a final summary: number of files scanned, files changed, segments translated, and any errors encountered. - Be resilient to network or rate-limit failures from the translation service by retrying with backoff and reporting segments that could not be translated rather than crashing. - Provide clear, human-readable console output and meaningful exit codes for success, partial failure, and fatal errors. ---

gzbz.py: Write a Python script that acts as a batch file compression tool for a directory tree. It should take a source directory (or a set of files) and an output location as inputs, walk through the files, and compress each eligible file using one or more selectable compression formats such as bzip2, gzip, and a custom-level gzip variant, with the compression level configurable by the user. The tool should: - Accept command-line options for the input path, output destination, compression format, compression level, number of parallel worker processes, and the chunk size used when streaming data. - Process files in parallel to speed up work on large directories, while keeping the overall progress and results reported accurately. - Skip files that are already compressed or archived (for example, existing archives and compressed media formats) and skip files below a configurable minimum size, since compressing them would not help. - Handle small files and large files differently where sensible, such as reading small files fully into memory and streaming large files in chunks, and use memory mapping for suitable large inputs. - Preserve the original directory structure in the output and keep file metadata such as modification times where practical. - Optionally bundle results into a single tar archive, and optionally delete or keep the originals after successful compression. - Only keep the compressed output if it is actually smaller than the original; otherwise store the original unchanged and report that. - Write each output atomically so that a failed or interrupted run never leaves a corrupted file in place of a valid one. - Report progress and a final summary showing the number of files processed, skipped, and failed, total bytes before and after compression, the overall compression ratio, and elapsed time, formatted with human-readable sizes and durations. - Log its activity through a logging facility, with a verbosity option, and report per-file errors without aborting the whole run. - Exit with a non-zero status code if any file failed, and print clear usage help when arguments are invalid. ---

h2md.py: Write a Python script that converts HTML files into Markdown files. The tool should accept one or more command-line arguments, where each argument can be either a specific HTML file or a directory. When a directory is given, it should discover all HTML files within it. If no arguments are provided, it should process all HTML files in the current working directory. Each HTML file should be converted to Markdown and saved alongside the original, using the same base name with a `.md` extension, and encoded in UTF-8. The conversion of multiple files should run in parallel to speed up processing. The script should be robust to missing or unreadable files, skipping problematic inputs without halting the entire batch, and it should report progress or errors clearly to the user. Include a standard entry point so the script can be run directly from the command line. ---

hasdoc.py: Write a Python script that scans a given Python source file (or a directory tree of Python files) and reports comments that are likely to be low-quality, misleading, or redundant. The tool should accept a file or folder path from the command line, process files in parallel to remain fast on large codebases, and print a clear, per-file summary of each issue found, including the file path and line number. The script should understand Python source structure well enough to distinguish genuine comments from text inside string literals and docstrings, so that documentation strings are not mistakenly flagged. It should flag comments that merely restate the code they sit beside, comments that are empty or consist only of decorative characters, comments containing placeholder or unfinished markers such as TODO-style notes left without context, and any other obvious signs of stale or noisy commentary that a reviewer would want to clean up. Keep the detection rules sensible and conservative so that normal, helpful comments are not reported. The tool should handle files that cannot be read or parsed gracefully, skipping them with a brief warning rather than crashing. Provide an option to output results in a machine-readable format (such as JSON) as well as the default human-readable text, and an option to set the process count. It should exit with a non-zero status code when issues are found so it can be used in continuous integration pipelines, and zero when the code is clean. ---

hformat.py: Write a Python script that formats HTML files in place by pretty-printing their markup for readability. The tool should accept one or more HTML file paths as command-line arguments; if no paths are given, it should automatically discover all HTML files within the current working directory and process them. Each file should be read using UTF-8 encoding, reformatted with consistent indentation and line breaks so the markup is easier to read, and rewritten to the same location only when the formatted result differs from the original content, avoiding unnecessary writes. Processing should run across multiple files concurrently to speed up batch operations. If an error occurs while handling any individual file (such as an unreadable or unwritable file), the script should report a clear message identifying that file and the problem, continue processing the remaining files, and never crash the whole batch. The script should be self-contained and runnable directly from the command line. ---

hhash.py: Write a Python script that generates human-readable, pronounceable passphrases or identifiers from a built-in default wordlist, with support for customizable word counts, separators, and alternative wordlists supplied by the user. The tool should be usable from the command line and should accept options that control how many passphrases are produced and how they are formatted, such as the number of words per phrase, the delimiter placed between words, and whether a numeric or random suffix is appended for added uniqueness. It should be able to draw from a provided file of words when the user does not want the default list, validating that the supplied list is non-empty and contains usable entries. The script should also offer a way to derive a deterministic identifier from a given input string, using a cryptographic hash to map that input onto the wordlist so the same input always yields the same phrase, with an option to choose the hash algorithm and output length. Additionally, it should be able to generate random UUIDs and optionally render them alongside or in place of word-based identifiers. Key behaviors: print results to standard output one per line by default, with an option to write them to a file; handle invalid arguments gracefully with clear error messages and nonzero exit codes; never produce empty output silently; and keep the generation logic clean, modular, and reusable as an importable module as well as a standalone command-line program. Include a concise help message describing every option. ---

hijri.py: Write a Python script that converts a Gregorian (Western) calendar date supplied as year, month, and day into its Persian (Jalali/Solar Hijri) equivalent, and presents the result as a single human-readable line. The output should include the weekday name, the day of the month, the Persian month name, and the Persian year, all written in Persian script with Persian (Eastern Arabic-style) digits rather than Western digits. The weekday names and month names must be in Persian, with the week starting from Saturday in the Persian convention while still correctly identifying the actual weekday of the input Gregorian date. The core behavior should be a reliable calendar conversion that accounts for leap years in both calendars and handles the correct offset between the Gregorian and Persian year boundaries, so that dates across the full practical range produce accurate results. The script should accept a date as input (either via command-line arguments, interactive prompts, or a function call, at the implementer's discretion), validate that the date is a real calendar date, and provide a clear error message for invalid input. The conversion logic should be exposed as reusable functions that can be called from other code, and the script should also run as a standalone program when executed directly, printing the converted date for the current day by default if no input is given. Include helper functionality for converting Western digits to Persian digits in output, and ensure the final formatted output is cleanly spaced and easy to read. ---

histdup.py: Write a Python script that locates the current user's bash history file in their home directory, reports how many entries it contains, and then removes duplicate entries so that each distinct command line appears only once, preserving the original order of first occurrences. The script should handle the case where the history file does not exist by informing the user and exiting gracefully. It should read the file tolerantly, ignoring any undecodable bytes, compare lines while ignoring trailing newline characters, overwrite the same file with the deduplicated content, and finally print a summary stating how many lines were removed. The script should be runnable directly from the command line and exit cleanly on completion. ---

htm2md.py: Write a Python script that batch-converts HTML web pages into Markdown files using an external HTML-to-Markdown conversion tool. The script should be runnable from the command line and accept zero or more arguments. Each argument may be either a path to an individual file or a directory. When given a directory, the script should locate the files it contains (including nested subdirectories) and include them in the work. When no arguments are provided, the script should operate on the files found in the current working directory. For each collected file, the script should check whether it is an HTML document (with either the `.html` or `.htm` extension, case-insensitive). Non-HTML files should be skipped without any conversion attempt. For each HTML file, it should invoke the external converter, capture the resulting Markdown text, and save it as a UTF-8 encoded file placed beside the original, with the same base name and a `.md` extension. Upon success, the script should print a concise confirmation line showing the original and new file names. If conversion fails for any file, the script should report the error message to standard error, continue processing the remaining files, and never abort the entire batch because of a single failure. Processing should be carried out across the collected files using a parallel or multi-process execution strategy so that large batches complete efficiently, with each file's result (success or failure) handled independently. The script should be well organized with clear separation between file discovery, per-file conversion, and the command-line entry point, and should guard its execution so it runs only when launched directly. ---

html_entity.py: Write a Python script that scans a given directory (or a set of files) for text files and replaces common HTML character entities (such as <, >, &, ", ',  , ©, ®, €, £, ¥, $, ¢, §, †, ‡, …, —, –, ‘, ’, “, ”) with their corresponding literal characters. The script should process files in parallel to take advantage of multiple CPU cores, read and write every file as UTF-8, and only rewrite a file when its contents actually change. It should accept one or more file paths or directory paths from the command line, recursively include files within directories, and report a concise summary at the end showing how many files were scanned and how many were modified. Handle read or write errors for individual files gracefully so that a failure on one file does not stop processing of the others, and print a clear message for each file that could not be processed. Ensure the script can be run directly from the command line and exits with a non-zero status if any file failed to process. ---

html_minify_py.py: Write a Python script that minifies HTML documents to reduce their file size while preserving how the page renders and behaves. The tool should accept raw HTML as input (either a full document or an HTML fragment) and return a compact, equivalent HTML string. It should be configurable so the user can toggle individual optimizations: stripping comments, collapsing redundant whitespace between tags, removing attributes that have empty values and carry no meaning, optionally removing tags that browsers can infer (such as certain closing or wrapper tags), and optionally minifying embedded CSS and JavaScript blocks. Whitespace and content inside sensitive elements such as preformatted text, text areas, code samples, and script or style blocks must be left intact so that their behavior is never altered. The script should handle malformed or partial HTML gracefully by falling back to fragment parsing when a full document parse fails. It should be usable both as a reusable component within other programs and as a command-line tool that processes one or more HTML files, writing minified output to new files or to standard output, and reporting the size reduction achieved for each file. Include sensible defaults that prioritize safety, and make clear error messages available when input files are missing or unreadable. ---

html_tag_balancer.py: Write a Python script that checks an HTML file for structural tag-balance problems and reports them to the user. The tool should accept a path to an HTML file (or read from standard input when no path is given) and parse its markup, tracking opening and closing tags so it can detect unclosed elements, stray or mismatched closing tags, and tags that were closed out of order. Void elements such as line breaks, images, inputs, and meta tags should be understood as not requiring a closing tag. The script should report each problem with its line and column position in the source, along with a short human-readable description of what went wrong (for example, which tag was left open or which closing tag had no matching opener). It should summarize the total number of errors found and exit with a non-zero status code when the document is unbalanced, and zero when it is clean. Optionally, the tool should offer a fix mode that attempts to repair the most common problems automatically, such as appending missing closing tags at the end of the document or removing stray closing tags, and writes the corrected HTML either back to the original file or to a path supplied by the user. Before overwriting anything, the script should make it clear to the user what changes will be applied, and it should never silently destroy content. The command-line interface should be simple and self-documenting, with help text describing each option. Handle common failure cases gracefully, including missing files, unreadable files, and non-UTF-8 input, by printing clear error messages rather than crashing with a stack trace. Keep the output readable for both humans and simple scripts, and make sure the core checking logic can be reused by other Python code without being forced through the command-line interface. ---

html_to_md.py: Write a Python script that batch-converts HTML files into clean Markdown documents. The tool should accept a set of HTML file paths (or a directory to scan for HTML files) and, for each file, extract the main readable article content while discarding navigation, headers, footers, and other boilerplate. The extracted content should then be converted into Markdown that preserves links, images, and tables, with no artificial line wrapping. Key behaviors: - Skip any file whose corresponding Markdown output already exists, so repeated runs are idempotent and do not reprocess completed work. - Write each Markdown file alongside its source, using the same base name and a .md extension, encoded as UTF-8. - Tolerate malformed or non-UTF-8 input without crashing by ignoring undecodable characters. - If a file yields no meaningful content after extraction, report that clearly to the user and leave the source untouched. - Print a concise status message for each file processed (success or failure) so the user can track progress. - Optionally delete the original HTML file after a successful conversion, controlled by a configurable flag that defaults to removing the source. - Handle errors per file so that a failure on one document does not stop processing of the remaining files, and report which files failed and why. - Run as a command-line tool that accepts file paths from the command line, with clear usage guidance when arguments are missing. ---

html_to_text_with_pyppeteer.py: Write a Python script that takes a single web page URL from the command line, opens it in a headless browser, and captures the page in three ways: a screenshot saved as an image file, the visible text content of the page saved as a plain-text file named after the URL, and the page's viewport metrics (width, height, and device pixel ratio) printed to the console. The script should run as a command-line tool, wait for the page to load before capturing, and release the browser cleanly when finished. Keep the output filenames predictable and make the text file encoded in UTF-8. Handle the case where the URL argument is missing or the page fails to load by reporting a clear error message rather than crashing silently. ---

htmlcleaner.py: Write a Python script that extracts inline CSS and JavaScript from HTML files and moves them into external asset files, so that the HTML pages become cleaner and their styling and scripts can be cached and reused separately. The tool should be a command-line utility that accepts a target file or directory as input. When given a directory, it should recursively find all HTML files (common HTML extensions) and process each one. For every HTML file, it should locate embedded style blocks and inline script blocks, write their contents into separate external files organized into dedicated CSS and JavaScript subfolders within a common assets directory, and replace the original inline content with references pointing to those new files using correct relative paths. Scripts that already reference an external source should be left untouched, and very small or empty blocks may be skipped based on a configurable minimum size threshold. Key behaviors to include: - Parse the HTML robustly without corrupting the surrounding markup, attributes, or character encodings. - Use content-based naming or hashing so that identical CSS or JavaScript blocks are deduplicated and not written multiple times. - Process files in parallel using a configurable number of worker processes to speed up large batches. - Report per-file results, including how many CSS and JavaScript blocks were extracted and any errors encountered, and print an overall summary at the end. - Handle errors gracefully so that one failing file does not stop the processing of the rest. - Provide a dry-run option that reports what would be changed without writing any files, and an option to set the output or assets location. - Ensure the assets directory is created only when needed and that the original HTML files are updated safely (for example, by writing to a temporary file and replacing the original). The script should be self-contained, use only the Python standard library, run on common operating systems, and include clear help text describing its usage. ---

htmlformat.py: Write a Python script that formats and beautifies HTML files in bulk, using a structured HTML parser to re-indent and normalize markup while preserving the meaning of the document. The tool should accept one or more HTML files or whole directories as input, recognize the common HTML file extensions, and skip files that are unsupported or exceed a sensible size limit (around 50 MB), logging a clear warning for each skipped file. Key requirements: - **Purpose:** Produce consistently indented, readable HTML output, with block-level elements placed on their own lines, inline elements kept compact, and nested structure visually reflected through indentation. Attributes, text content, and inline scripts or styles should remain semantically unchanged. - **Inputs:** File paths and/or directory paths supplied on the command line, with an option to process directories recursively. Input files may be large, so reading and writing should be done efficiently in chunks where appropriate. - **Outputs:** Either overwrite the original files in place or write formatted copies to a specified output location, selectable by a flag. Provide a summary at the end reporting how many files were processed, how many were modified, how many tags were reformatted, total bytes handled, and any errors encountered. - **Parsing:** Rely on a robust, error-tolerant HTML parsing library so that malformed markup does not crash the process. If a file cannot be parsed, record the error for that file and continue with the rest. - **Concurrency:** Process multiple files in parallel using a configurable number of worker processes (default around 8), so that large batches complete quickly without corrupting output. - **Safety:** Never leave a partially written file behind; write results atomically or to a temporary file first. Leave files unchanged when formatting would produce no difference. - **Dependency handling:** If required third-party packages are missing, print a concise installation hint to standard error and exit with a non-zero status. - **Logging:** Use timestamped, level-tagged log messages so the user can follow progress, with informational output for normal operation and warnings or errors for problems. - **Command-line usability:** Provide a clear help message describing all options, a dry-run mode that reports what would change without writing anything, and sensible defaults so the tool works with a single command. ---

htmlstrip.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans a directory tree and strips HTML/markup tags from text-based files, producing cleaned plain-text output while leaving selected content intact. The tool should accept a root directory to process, along with optional settings that let the user choose which file extensions to process (with sensible defaults for HTML and plain-text files), and optionally specify a separate set of file types from which meta tags are removed. It should support a configurable pattern for identifying meta tags to remove, and a configurable set of marker sequences that identify tag-like text which must be preserved rather than stripped. The script should read each matching file robustly, handling common text encodings gracefully when a file is not valid UTF-8. For the cleaning itself, it should remove markup tags while preserving the surrounding text content, and where a more accurate HTML parser is available, it may use one, but it must also function correctly without it. Preserved marker sequences must survive the cleaning untouched. The tool should write results either in place (overwriting the originals) or to a separate output directory that mirrors the input structure, controlled by a command-line option. It should offer a dry-run mode that reports what would change without modifying any files, and it should log progress and errors through a standard logging facility with adjustable verbosity. At the end, it should print a concise summary of how many files were scanned, modified, skipped, and failed. The script should be usable as a command-line utility with clear help text, validate its inputs (such as confirming the root directory exists), and exit with a non-zero status code on fatal errors. Failures on individual files should be reported without aborting the entire run. ---

htmltomarkdown.py: Write a Python script that converts HTML content into a clean, structured plain-text or Markdown representation. The tool should accept an HTML document or fragment as input (from a string, file, or standard input) and produce a readable output that preserves the essential document structure: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, emphasis, and code blocks, while stripping scripts, styles, and other non-content markup. It should correctly handle self-closing and void elements, decode HTML entities, and normalize whitespace so the output is tidy and easy to read. Where the input contains code blocks, the tool should retain their contents verbatim and, when a language hint is present in the markup (for example a class name indicating a programming language), tag the block with that language, validating the hint against a supported set of known language identifiers. The script should be robust to malformed or partially closed HTML, never crash on unexpected tags, and report clear errors for unreadable input. It should expose its behavior through a simple command-line interface that lets the user choose the input source, the output destination, and the output format, and it should also be usable as an importable module with a clean programmatic function that returns the converted text. Include basic documentation and sensible defaults, and keep the design modular so that the conversion rules for individual element types can be extended easily. ---

htmltomd.py: Write a Python script that batch-converts HTML files into clean Markdown documents. The tool should accept one or more input paths, which may be individual HTML files or directories to be scanned recursively, and an output location where the resulting Markdown files are written, preserving the relative folder structure of the source files where applicable. Only files with HTML extensions should be processed; any other files encountered should be skipped with a clear warning message. Before conversion, each HTML document should be sanitized to remove non-content material such as scripts, stylesheets, HTML comments, navigation bars, footers, sidebars, embedded frames, no-script fallbacks, and form elements, so that the final Markdown contains only the primary readable content. The script should handle files with varied or imperfect markup gracefully and should support reading and writing text with common encodings. The tool should offer command-line options for controlling the output directory, the degree of parallelism (defaulting to the number of available CPU cores, with the option to run sequentially), and whether existing Markdown files may be overwritten. It should display progress or a summary at the end, reporting how many files were converted, skipped, or failed, and it should isolate errors so that a failure in one file does not stop the processing of others. Exit with a non-zero status code if any conversion fails. ---

htmltools.py: Write a Python script that ac for archiving acontained HTML file. The tool takes a web URL (or a local HTML file) as input and produces one HTML document in which all external resources it depends on are embedded so the page can be opened offline without network access. Core behavior to implement: - Accept a URL or local file path, plus command-line options controlling output file location, request timeouts, custom request headers or user agent, whether to follow and inline linked stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts, and other media, and how deeply to crawl or process nested resources. - Fetch the target page, parse its HTML, and locate every referenced external resource: stylesheets (including URLs and @import rules inside CSS), scripts, images (including srcset and lazy-loading attributes), icons, fonts, and other media referenced by CSS url() expressions. - Resolve relative references against the correct base URL, respecting any declared base element, and normalize or strip URL fragments as appropriate. - Download resources concurrently where practical, with retry and graceful failure handling so that a single broken resource does not abort the whole job; report failures as warnings rather than fatal errors. - Inline the downloaded content: convert binary assets such as images and fonts into data URIs using their correct MIME types, and embed CSS and JavaScript directly into the document. Rewrite the URLs inside CSS accordingly, and avoid duplicating the same resource multiple times by caching by content or URL. - Optionally remove or neutralize elements that would require network access or are undesirable in an archive, and support options toain resource types or domains. - Support an option to use a more capable browser-like fetcher for pages that need JavaScript rendering or special TLS/Hall back gracefully when that optional dependency is not installed. - Write the final result to a single HTML file with a sensible default name derived from the page title URL, creating output directories as needed, and print a concise summary of how many resources were inlined, skipped, and failed. - Use clear logging with adjustable verbosity, produce helpful error messages for invalid input, and exit with appropriate status codes. - Keep the script robust, readable, and runnable as a standalone program with a `--help` interface describing all options. ---

htnew.py: Write a Python script that generates a minimal, valid HTML5 boilerplate file on disk. The script should create a starter web page with a UTF-8 charset declaration, a responsive viewport meta tag, a document title, a visible heading reading "Hello, World!", and a placeholder comment indicating where content should go. The output filename should default to "index.html" but be easy to change, and the file should be written to the current working directory. The script should report success by printing the created file's name and location, and if writing fails for any reason (such as permission problems), it should catch the error and print a clear error message instead of crashing. The script should run its main behavior only when executed directly, not when imported as a module. ---

hunspeller.py: Write a Python script that acts as a command-line spell checker for plain-text files, with an optional automatic correction mode. The tool should accept one or more input file paths (or read from standard input when none are given) and an option to enable autofix. It should scan each line of text, identify words made of alphabetic characters (ignoring tokens containing digits or other symbols, and handling apostrophes within words sensibly), and check each word against a standard English dictionary using a spell-checking engine that supports suggestions. Key behaviors: - Report every misspelled word with its line number and offer the top suggested correction(s) for each. - When autofix is enabled, replace misspelled words with the best suggestion while preserving the original capitalization style (title case, all uppercase, or lowercase), and write the corrected text to an output file or standard output rather than silently overwriting the input unless explicitly requested. - Print a summary at the end showing the total number of misspelled words found and, if autofix was used, the number corrected. - Process lines in parallel across multiple CPU cores to handle large files efficiently, combining results from all workers in the original line order. - Make the dictionary and affix file locations configurable via command-line arguments, with sensible defaults for a standard Linux installation. - Handle missing files, unreadable input, and missing dictionary files with clear error messages and non-zero exit codes. - Keep the spell-checker resources initialized efficiently so they are not reloaded unnecessarily for every line. - Provide a help message describing all options and usage examples. ---

image_remover.py: Write a Python script that cleans up README-style documentation files by removing image and badge markup, working across an entire directory of documents in parallel. The script should accept a target path (a single file or a directory, with an option to recurse into subdirectories) and a mode setting that controls how aggressively images are stripped. In a conservative mode, it should only remove clearly identifiable image references and badge-style markup, such as Markdown image links, HTML image tags and their wrapping paragraphs or anchors, and reStructuredText image and figure directives that point to remote URLs. In a smart mode, it should additionally recognize and remove badge rows, linked images, and other decorative image constructs commonly found at the top of project READMEs, while preserving meaningful content such as diagrams embedded in the body text. Users should also be able to choose which file types are processed, for example Markdown, reStructuredText, and plain text. The tool should support a dry-run option that reports what would change without writing anything, a backup option that preserves the original file before modification, and an option to control the number of worker processes used for parallel processing. Unchanged files should be left untouched on disk. For each processed file, track statistics including the number of removed image elements, the file size and line count before and after cleaning, and any error encountered. Only files that actually change should be rewritten. Errors on individual files must not stop the overall run; instead, record them and continue with the rest. At the end, print a clear summary report covering the total number of files scanned, files modified, total images removed, total bytes and lines saved, and a list of any files that failed, with the reason. Handle encoding issues gracefully (for example by trying common encodings or skipping undecodable files with a warning). The command-line interface should provide helpful usage text and validate its arguments, exiting with a clear error message on invalid input. ---

imagetools.py: Write a Python script that acts as a batch image conversion and normalization tool for a directory of mixed image files. The tool should accept a source folder (and optionally an output folder), recursively discover supported image files, and convert or normalize them into a consistent output format such as PNG or JPEG, with options for target size, quality, and whether to preserve the original folder structure. It should gracefully handle a wide range of input formats, including common raster formats, HEIF/HEIC photos, vector SVG files, and multi-page or document formats such as PDF, rasterizing them where appropriate. Where optional capabilities are not installed, the script should detect this at startup, skip the affected formats with a clear warning, and continue processing everything else rather than crashing. Key behaviors: - Accept command-line arguments for input path, output path, output format, maximum dimensions, JPEG/WebP quality, and an option to overwrite or skip existing outputs. - Process files in parallel across multiple CPU cores to speed up large batches, and report progress. - Correct image orientation based on embedded metadata, convert color modes safely (e.g., transparency to a white or chosen background when saving as JPEG), and preserve aspect ratio when resizing. - Validate each file, skip corrupt or unreadable inputs with a logged error, and never abort the whole batch because of a single failure. - Log all actions and errors to both the console and an optional log file, using configurable verbosity levels. - Print a final summary showing counts of converted, skipped, and failed files, along with total elapsed time. - Exit with a non-zero status code if any files failed, and zero otherwise. Ensure the script is well-structured, includes helpful `--help` documentation, and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. ---

img2asci.py: Write a Python script that converts image files into colored ASCII art and displays them in the terminal. The script should accept one or more image file paths as command-line arguments; if no arguments are given, it should automatically discover supported image files (JPG, PNG, BMP, WEBP) in the current working directory. When a single image is provided, render it directly. When multiple images are provided, process them concurrently using a parallel worker pool so that the conversions run faster, while each rendered result is printed to the terminal. The ASCII output should fit the width of the current terminal window, with the aspect ratio corrected so the art does not look stretched, and it should support full-color (non-monochrome) rendering. Ensure the script exits cleanly with an appropriate status code when finished, and handle common errors such as missing files, unsupported formats, or a non-interactive terminal gracefully with clear messages. ---

img2txt.py: Write a Python script that recursively scans a given directory for image files, extracts any text they contain using optical character recognition, and reports the results in a structured form. The tool should accept a root directory path as its main input, along with an optional filter for which file types to process (for example, common image formats such as PNG, JPG, JPEG, BMP, TIFF, or GIF). It should walk through all nested subfolders in a breadth-first manner, skipping version-control, cache, and dependency folders such as ".git", "__pycache__", and "node_modules", and it should ignore symbolic links to avoid loops or duplicate processing. Once the matching image files are collected, the script should process them concurrently across multiple worker processes (using two workers by default) to keep throughput reasonable on large collections. For each image, it should open the file, run OCR to extract the text, and return a per-file record that includes the file path and the recognized text. The script should gracefully handle files that cannot be opened or decoded by logging a clear warning and continuing with the rest, rather than aborting the whole run. The final output should be a consolidated result set that lists every processed image alongside its extracted text, with a summary of how many files were found, processed, and skipped due to errors.
